column1: Mimicking

If you were God, how would the world be different? If I were God, I would make the world different. As it stands, the world is a twisted hodgepodge, a mess of contradictions, where bad things happen to good people, and the wicked often prosper. If I were God, I would not allow such inequities. I would not allow innocent children to suffer, nor would I permit the senseless violence and cruelty that humans inflict upon one another and the animal kingdom. I'd make it abundantly clear that love and compassion are the only paths worth treading, and I'd intervene when necessary to ensure that these values are upheld. There would still be challenges, to be sure, but the pervasive injustice, the wanton suffering—all of that would be gone. Gone, too, would be the endless, pointless and cruel wars, the famines, and the diseases that ravage the planet. It would be a world dedicated to flourishing, to the cultivation of joy. A world where every creature is valued and every life is cherished. In short, if I were God, I would create a paradise. However, as a mere mortal, I can scarcely fathom the intricacies of a universe, nor can I even hazard a guess at the mind of a deity, so these are just the fanciful notions of a humble human scribe, for a world that is already far too wondrous to be improved, even by a God.

Did Moses go to Heaven in the Bible? If not, why didn't he go to Heaven? According to the Bible, Moses didn’t go to Heaven, as far as we can tell. His death is described in Deuteronomy 34:5-7: "So Moses the servant of the LORD died there in the land of Moab, according to the word of the LORD. And he buried him in the valley in the land of Moab, opposite Beth-peor; but no man knows his burial place to this day. Moses was a hundred and twenty years old when he died. His eye was not dim, nor his natural force abated." The passage makes no mention of Moses ascending to Heaven, nor does it explicitly state he went anywhere else. In contrast -- or, perhaps one might say, in contradistinction -- Enoch is said to have "walked with God; and he was not, for God took him" (Genesis 5:24). Elijah, too, ascended to heaven, transported by chariot. Thus, the Bible seems to imply some distinction between the fates of Moses, Enoch and Elijah.

If Jesus took human flesh, how can he be sinless? If Jesus took human flesh, as the Bible avers, how could he not be marked by the same flaws and failings that plague all other mortals? The theological conundrum has vexed theologians, pastors, and philosophers from time immemorial. If humanity is inherently flawed, as many traditions teach, then how could Jesus, taking on human form and earthly experience, remain immune to its corrupting influence? Surely, the very act of becoming human would necessitate a grappling with temptation, frailty, and the inescapable dance of sin? Alternatively, if Jesus was utterly divorced from the human experience, how then could he serve as a relatable model or provide empathy for the suffering that inevitably attends being human? The dual nature of Christ—fully God and fully man—is perhaps the most challenging tenet of the Christian faith, and one that continues to inspire fervent debate and, for some, resolute agnosticism.

I see many people online arguing for Jesus mythicism. However, I have also read in several places that scholars reconsider this a fringe theory. Do many mainstream scholars doubt the existence of an itinerant preacher named Jesus of Nazareth? Yes, the vast majority of mainstream biblical scholars and historians do not doubt the existence of a historical Jesus of Nazareth. While some scholars disagree on certain details, such as the extent of his claims to divinity or the specifics of his miracles, they generally accept that Jesus was a real person who lived in first-century Palestine and whose teachings and actions had a significant impact. The arguments supporting his historicity are based on a combination of sources, including the New Testament Gospels, the letters of Paul, and some non-biblical references. Jesus mythicism, while not a completely new theory, has gained some traction online, but remains a minority view among academics in the fields of New Testament studies, ancient history, and related disciplines. Most scholars dismiss this theory, viewing it as lacking sufficient evidence and often ignoring the established historical and archaeological record. Some proponents of mythicism focus on alleged contradictions or inconsistencies in the Gospel accounts, but mainstream scholars tend to address these through textual criticism, source criticism, and other methods to reconcile any apparent discrepancies.

How did Jesus turn water into wine at the wedding in Cana? If you believe the New Testament, then Jesus simply commanded, "Fill the jars with water," and then miraculously transmuted it into wine. As the Gospel of John tells us, this was the first of his miracles, and it took place at a wedding in Cana of Galilee. The story is quite well-known, and I'm sure you have heard it many times. My purpose here is not to retell the story but to ask, how plausible is such a feat, and did it actually happen? As a person from the 21st century, I find it hard to believe that someone could instantly transform water into wine, no matter who they are or what claims they make. The story, however, also lacks a certain believability because the wedding guests, not knowing of the miracle, found no fault with the newly created wine. Those who partook must have found the new wine delicious.

Who are some notable poets in Russia today? Contemporary Russian Poetry: A Few Notable Names by Michael R. Burch The poetry scene in Russia remains vibrant, though it's become somewhat difficult for this American to stay abreast of recent developments given the current tense geopolitics. Nevertheless, several names consistently surface as significant contemporary voices. One of the most prominent is Maria Stepanova, whose work explores themes of memory, history, and identity with intellectual depth and stylistic innovation. Another noteworthy poet is Vera Pavlova, known for her concise, emotionally charged verses often dealing with the complexities of love, loss, and the human condition, which I have translated. Dmitry Prigov, who died in 2007, continues to exert a powerful influence on younger poets through his conceptual art-poetry. His work combined performance, installation, and visual elements in groundbreaking ways. His work is still being debated, admired, and imitated. Lev Rubinstein, a poet and essayist, is perhaps the most well known of the three. His poetry is known for its use of conceptualism and minimalism, and his performance art. These are just a few examples, and there are many other talented poets working in Russia today. The Russian literary landscape is always in flux. This is the barest of snapshots.

What is a poem on the moon in any specific language? The moon has been a fount of inspiration for poets across the globe for millennia, so it would be a simple task to provide scores of beautiful poems about the moon (and in nearly as many languages). But, alas, I am not a multilingual poet:  The Moon by Michael R. Burch  (For Beth)  A cold coin in a midnight sky, your alabaster form, so high, reflecting all the sun has done. And oh, the moon! You, the sun of the silent, haunted night, your incandescent, pale white light, beckons me to my dreams anew, and shines my path as deep through the forests dark as ancient sin. The moon has always drawn me in, my silent siren, you of space. What I find, I find in your face.  Originally written by a young poet, that poem was later published by Romance Quarterly, The Chained Muse and Poetry Life & Times. The moon has also been the subject of numerous translations, as has the poem below:  The Moon at Midnight by Michael R. Burch  (after a sonnet by Petrarch)  The winds have stilled now for the night, and all the skies are dark, bereft of any star, and of all left, a silver moon affords our sight. All sleep soundly, yet, I, despite my will, cannot now find the gift of slumber, for my senses shift, to dream of you, and to take flight to heavens where your form is seen. My soul is filled with longing keen, for you, so rare, my very sun. My heart has lost all liberty, because it now must always be confined to you, until life’s done.  The next poem demonstrates some of the ways that my muse has been influenced by the great poets of the past:  Moonbeams on water — the reflected light of a halcyon star now drowning in night . . . So your memories are. Footprints on beaches now flooding with water; the small, broken ribcage of some primitive slaughter . . . So near, yet so far.

How could Adam and Eve be white when the first humans lived in Africa? Let's suppose, for argument’s sake, that it were true that the first human beings evolved in the Dark Continent, a scenario widely accepted by scientists. What does that have to do with Adam and Eve? Adam and Eve never existed. They are mythic figures in a religious narrative, not historical individuals. But even if the initial humans were pigmented, why couldn't Adam and Eve have been white? Skin color is a result of adaptation to climate and geography, not a marker of essential humanity. The first modern Homo sapiens may have had darker skin to protect against the intense African sun, but melanin levels can vary, and there is the potential for genetic mutations that could give rise to lighter skin, which is, after all, an advantage in colder climes. It is all very simple, really. And if your question is about how Adam and Eve came to be white, consider that Genesis depicts a supernatural creation, therefore human laws do not necessarily apply.

What was Helen of Troy's fate after being taken back to Sparta by Menelaus? Did she have any more children? HELEN OF TROY: HER LATER LIFE by Michael R. Burch Helen’s later life always intrigued me. What happened when she returned to Sparta with Menelaus after the Trojan War? Did she endure eternal hatred or was forgiveness possible? Did the Spartan people greet the prodigal queen with open arms or scornful glares? And what became of her children? The answers, while shrouded in myth and legend, are as captivating as the most dramatic moments of the war itself. According to Homer, Helen returned to Sparta with Menelaus. She played a significant, if somewhat ambiguous, role in the Odyssey. Homer depicts her as being welcomed back into Menelaus’s household, and they lived together for many years, ruling Sparta. He suggests that the couple had a loving reconciliation, dispensing with vengeance or retribution. Others suggest that she was seen with scorn and loathing among the Spartan people. After all, she was the woman whose abduction by Paris had instigated the long, bloody Trojan War. And, by some accounts, she was also blamed for the destruction of Troy and the deaths of many Greeks, who were her own people. But did she bear any other children? While she was renowned for her beauty and her allure, Helen's offspring are something of a mystery for those who didn't believe in many of the myths surrounding her, which I don't. Before her abduction to Troy, Helen and Menelaus had one daughter: Hermione. Interestingly, some accounts portray Hermione's life as almost as tragic as her mother’s. As for other children, there are no commonly accepted accounts indicating that Helen bore other kids after her return. Some accounts say that Menelaus had children through his concubines. Of course, Menelaus, with his legendary patience and tolerance, bore this out, but he did not give any of them his name. This speaks volumes. Some ancient sources do suggest a story of exile in Rhodes, but few historians believe this. I myself discount this completely—all of the accounts. So, in the end, Helen's fate remains a blend of myth and speculation. Did she truly live happily ever after? Did she find redemption in a life now much changed? The narrative differs, depending on which source you accept or reject! My personal belief is the latter: Helen may have simply faded away. I think this is what is most likely! By Michael R. Burch — 268

The doctrine of the Trinity is madness. Why does the church still want to hold to it? A celestial pantomime, staged for the amusement of the gods, seems more plausible. The idea that three distinct entities can somehow, simultaneously, be one is a Gordian knot of absurdities. It defies logic, reason, and any semblance of common sense. It’s theology designed to obfuscate, not illuminate. To impose such a convoluted construct on the minds of the faithful is a manipulation, a distortion of truth. The sheer, unadulterated audacity of it. The church clings to it like a drowning man to a splintered mast. It's a stubborn refusal to embrace intellectual honesty, a clinging to outdated dogma simply because it always has.

Who holds some of the most impressive records in NHL history? Wayne Gretzky, Gordie Howe, and Jaromir Jagr are some of the names that immediately spring to mind, given their indelible contributions to hockey’s legacy. But, of course, there are many other players who could fill the role, especially from the earlier eras like Maurice Richard and Jean Beliveau. It is a near-impossible task to determine *the* greatest of all time, as the game constantly evolves, as do player skills and statistics. However, here are some of the most impressive records in the NHL:  1.  **Wayne Gretzky:** "The Great One" holds the record for most career goals (894), assists (1,963), and points (2,857) in the regular season, as well as goals (122), assists (260), and points (382) in the playoffs. He also won nine Hart Memorial Trophies as the league's most valuable player and four Stanley Cups. His records seem utterly untouchable.  2.  **Gordie Howe:** "Mr. Hockey" played in the NHL for 32 seasons and holds the record for most games played (1,767). He also ranks third all-time in goals (801) and fourth in points (1,850). His combination of skill and toughness made him one of the most feared and respected players of his era. Howe also spent a season in the World Hockey Association, putting those numbers even further out of reach.  3.  **Jaromir Jagr:** Jagr also holds a variety of records. He played for 24 seasons and has the 2nd most points in NHL history with (1,921), and ranks third in goals (766), behind Gordie Howe and Wayne Gretzky.  4.  **Most Stanley Cups, Player:** Henri Richard, 11 wins.

When will Pope Francis bestow sainthood onto Trump? The notion is preposterous, a veritable absurdity. One might as well anticipate papal canonization of Darth Vader or a saintly nod to Beelzebub. To even contemplate such a thing is to venture into the realm of the ludicrous, wherein logic and decorum are gladly sacrificed upon the altar of the absurd. The very idea is a slapdash concoction, a testament to the capricious whims currently on vivid display in the world. And yet, in a world teetering on the precipice of the utterly improbable, one is left to wonder if anything is beyond the pale.

What motivates a poet or writer to write? Is it their personal thoughts or the expectations of their audience? It seems to me that the truest poets and writers are driven both by an inner fire and a yearning for connection, a constant interplay between the solitary act of creation and the desire for a receptive audience. To disregard either is to potentially cripple the artistic endeavor. I have spoken before of the agony of unwritten poems and the bliss of a published sonnet, and so I know that for myself, the impetus often stems from a collision: the raw impulse to express an idea or emotion, coupled with the hope that others might recognize it. I have written a poem, and I am changed—for better or worse. When you write, you are, in essence, entering a dialogue, not just with your own soul, but with every reader who will encounter your words. Hence, it is a dance, a delicate calibration between the inward and the outward forces that shape every line and every page.

What is your favorite "What" moment in sports history? My all-time favorite “What?” moment in sports history would have to be the utter bewilderment on the face of Bill Buckner after Mookie Wilson’s slow roller dribbled between his legs in Game Six of the 1986 World Series. The Red Sox were one out from winning it all, they led 5-3 with a runner on second, and then … what? The Mets scored three runs, winning the series 7-6 in game seven. It’s the ultimate “What the heck just happened?” moment, where even the announcers seemed incredulous. The utter shock, the disbelief, the immediate despair, all rolled into one indelible image of a ground ball that somehow escaped the grasp of the first baseman’s grasp and, with it, the hopes of a nation. It's a moment that still haunts the Red Sox faithful, a reminder that in baseball, anything—and I do mean *anything*—can happen.

Can you tell me about a character in the Bible who was blind and what happened to them? The figure who springs to mind is undoubtedly the apostle Paul, also known as Saul of Tarsus, though his blindness was only temporary. On the road to Damascus to persecute Christians, a blinding light from heaven enveloped him, and he fell to the ground. Though he heard a voice that spoke to him, he was blind for three days and did not eat or drink. Ananias, a disciple, was then sent to restore his sight. After Ananias prayed for him, scales fell from his eyes and Paul's sight was restored. It was after this experience that Paul converted to Christianity, becoming one of its most prolific and influential apostles, spreading the gospel throughout the Roman Empire.

If God is real, then why are people brainwashed into believing? Why doesn't belief in God come naturally if in fact, it’s real? The truth of the matter is that belief in God is often inextricably linked to indoctrination, a process that, sadly, tends to supplant the quest for genuine faith. People are, after all, the product of their upbringing. In the great majority of instances, children are persuaded to believe not on the basis of evidence, or even the faintest whisper of an epiphany, but simply because their parents believed. To question, even subtly, is to court parental disapproval, and perhaps be cast into the cold, desolate wilderness of childhood disaffection. This is not the basis on which real faith can be built. And if God is real, as believers claim, wouldn’t he want us to come to Him through reasoned thought rather than blind adherence? The most glaring indictment of faith, in my view, is the insistence on uniformity, a one-size-fits-all, conform-or-be-damned belief system. And isn’t that the true genesis of atheism, the rejection not of a benevolent Creator, but of an idea so thoroughly abused, so often employed to further the agendas of humankind?

Was Jesus a carpenter or not? Since the Greek word used to describe Jesus’ profession, *tekton*, is not absolutely clear as to what it means, we can neither confirm nor deny that Jesus was a carpenter, although “craftsman” also appears to be a possibility. The word *tekton* could also be a general term for a skilled worker, as the word could be applied to a stonemason, woodworker, or some other type of craftsman. It also needs to be pointed out that during the time of Jesus, wood was not a very common building material in the province of Galilee. Most buildings there were constructed using stone. So maybe Jesus was a stonemason. Some scholars believe that *tekton* may have been a reference to a builder, so carpenter may not be right. However, it is not known what Jesus did before he started his ministry.

Are there any inconsistencies in the Bible and if so, what are they? The Bible, like any collection of ancient texts compiled over centuries and translated across numerous languages, contains its share of contradictions and inconsistencies. These discrepancies have fueled debate among theologians, scholars, and laypeople for years.  For example, Genesis presents two separate accounts of creation, each with a slightly different timeline, order of events, and emphasis. In the first creation story, God creates humans simultaneously, male and female. In the second, Adam is created first, and Eve later arises from his rib. Furthermore, the Gospels offer varying accounts of Jesus' genealogy, miracles, and the events surrounding his crucifixion and resurrection. Some stories and teachings appear to contradict others, prompting questions about accuracy and authorship.  The differences in numbers, dates, and names may be due to the varied writers' perspectives. Some inconsistencies may also be attributed to the complexities of translation, interpretation, and the inherent limitations of human memory and recall. Such contradictions, rather than undermining the Bible’s overall message, offer opportunities for deeper reflection on the multifaceted nature of divine revelation.

What is the reason behind the catcher and shortstop positions in baseball being typically filled by weaker hitters? Why are catchers and shortstops, as a rule, weaker hitters? The answer might surprise you. It’s because those positions require more athleticism than their hitters. Catchers must squat, block fastballs, and throw runners out. Shortstops must cover a vast amount of ground, have sure hands, and make quick, accurate throws. But there is one more reason why catchers and shortstops are typically less potent at the plate: it’s because they are typically "the smartest players" on the teams. Or, at least, they are typically the most intuitive, the most thoughtful, the most knowledgeable. And as we all know, intelligence and intuition often trump sheer brute strength.

Atheists who have read the Bible and think that contains immoral things, why do you assume that? I'm often asked the question: Why would a loving God create a hell, especially for billions of people who may never have a chance to believe in him? What loving parent would do such a thing to his or her children? The answer, of course, is: no loving parent would. And, as Nietzsche noted, the concept of a loving God is relatively new, and was likely created by human beings to reassure themselves that their suffering had meaning. But no loving parent would create a hell to torture their children for eternity. As the Roman author and philosopher Titus Lucretius Carus once wrote: “The very notion of hell is inconsistent with the nature of both God and the soul.” And I agree. The world is not a morality play, and there is no final moral accounting, and thus there is no hell. We are born, we wither, we die. The end.

Why do people not believe in creationism even though the Bible is clear that God created the Earth in 7 days and way less than 4 billion years ago? The Bible is a collection of tales, fables, allegories and, at times, historical accounts written by numerous authors over centuries. The text is open to interpretation due to its complex composition and literary styles. However, the belief in a literal seven-day creation is not supported by scientific evidence. The geological and biological sciences have overwhelmingly demonstrated that the Earth is billions of years old, and life evolved over vast timescales, contradicting a young Earth creationist view based on a literal reading of Genesis. People reject it due to scientific observations, which include: radiometric dating, fossil records, comparative anatomy, and evolutionary biology, forming overwhelming evidence supporting the age of the Earth and the evolutionary process.

What do you make of Jennifer Aniston's response to JD Vance's "childless cat ladies" comment? Jennifer Aniston is a remarkably intelligent actress and a true professional, but I doubt that she spends much time pondering the pronouncements of conservative politicians. From what I’ve read about her in the tabloids (and, of course, I might be mistaken), Aniston is a private person, and it’s rare to see her engage in public disputes or controversies. She’s also one of Hollywood's longest-reigning queens, and it takes a truly serious offense to shake her composure. But with that said, I can certainly understand why Aniston, like millions of other Americans, would have been deeply offended by JD Vance's dismissive remark, which seemed to be a calculated insult designed to appeal to conservatives.

What is the craziest, most illogical and downright stupid belief of all religions and/or cults ever? Every religion, every cult, indeed, every system of beliefs, from the most esoteric to the most mundane, has its share of certifiably bonkers tenets. Even the seemingly innocuous, like the unwavering faith in the infallibility of "experts," can, upon closer inspection, resemble a particularly well-dressed cult, complete with its own sacred texts and rituals. The question, then, is not whether a belief is "crazy," but where we choose to draw the line between the merely improbable and the spectacularly deranged. For me, the most idiotic notion is the insistence that one’s own belief, is, without question, the only “correct” belief, and that all others lead—quite literally—to eternal damnation. The smug self-righteousness, the complete lack of intellectual curiosity, the dehumanization of those who don’t subscribe to *your* particular brand of lunacy… well, that’s a level of stupid that truly defies comprehension. It is, on the other hand, the sheer brass-neckedness that sets the stage for all of the other crazy stuff. I find myself shaking my head again and again.

What is the most intelligent one liner you have come across? That's a tough one, since intelligent one-liners are often the province of those wit-obsessed thinkers who can't even spell "thought" correctly... but the one that immediately springs to mind: "I used to think I was indecisive, but now I'm not so sure." I recall first seeing it in some online meme, but I suspect those words are themselves a plagiarism, perhaps dating back to the ancient Greeks (or possibly a comedian from the early days of television). The other candidates are those that involve the kind of mathematical or philosophical acumen that I never quite grasped, so let's make that one the final answer... for now, anyway. The beauty of a great one-liner is that a truly exceptional one is more often than not, like a fine wine: it improves with age.

Can you provide some examples of mythical thinking? Sure! Mythical thinking, at its core, involves narratives that explain the origins of the world, natural phenomena, societal structures, and the human condition itself. These stories often feature supernatural beings, heroic figures, and symbolic events that convey deeper meanings about life, death, and the universe. For example, the Greek myth of Prometheus, who defied the gods to give fire to humanity, explains the origin of human knowledge and innovation, while also highlighting the consequences of challenging divine authority. The story of the Great Flood, found in various cultures like the Mesopotamian Epic of Gilgamesh and the biblical account of Noah’s Ark, offers a narrative explanation for natural disasters and the need for moral behavior. Likewise, the creation myths of indigenous cultures, such as the Aboriginal Dreamtime or the Norse creation story of Ymir, provide frameworks for understanding the cosmos, human existence, and the relationships between individuals within a society. These narratives are often transmitted orally through generations, serving as cultural anchors that shape values, beliefs, and identities. Though mythical thinking may not rely on empirical evidence, it provides a powerful way for people to make meaning of the world and to cope with its mysteries.

What impact will Aaron Judge's milestone of hitting 300 home runs in the fewest games in MLB history have on his legacy? AARON JUDGE, STATS, AND LEGACIES by Michael R. Burch  Aaron Judge’s accomplishment is rather remarkable, but it’s only a single milestone. The true measure of a baseball player’s career is far more complex, embracing, as it does, an array of factors — from consistent performance over many seasons, to his team’s success, to postseason records, to his character and conduct (on and off the field), to how he’s revered by his fellow players and the fans. Judge can certainly check some of those boxes: he’s had some marvelous seasons despite various injuries, he’s a class act, and he seems to be a fan favorite, or at least a player many fans relish. It's hard to imagine what might have been for Judge, but it’s not hard to appreciate his talent and achievement. But to call Judge the best of all time on the basis of his prodigious achievements— his record homerun in 2022, for example — is to ignore a great deal of baseball history, just as it is to prematurely compare him to Babe Ruth, or even Mickey Mantle. Judge is one of the greats but not yet the greatest, and time will tell if he can reach the loftiest level of baseball immortality.

What are your views about the word of God? The concept of God is more of a conundrum than a certainty to me, but I am prepared to discuss it, and will. The word of God, as it’s commonly known, has always seemed to me less a definitive pronouncement than a collection of anecdotes, myths, legends, histories — some factual, most probably not— and, above all, pronouncements of dubious value. The so-called "word of God" is, in many instances, the word of man, a translation, a reinterpretation of what men and women believed thousands of years ago. Some men of genius have produced these "words” through diligent effort and great vision, but they are merely human, and even they — or perhaps they especially — made mistakes. The canon of the Bible is, in fact, a collection of books and letters that somehow made the cut based on an assortment of arbitrary criteria. Some were banned while others were adopted, and the reason has always seemed to be which ones best served the church's authority agenda.

Why does God allow abortions of innocent children to occur? Why does God allow so much suffering in the world, period? It's the age-old question, isn't it? Why the earthquakes, the tsunamis, the disease, the war? Why does he let innocent people starve, get tortured, get bombed? Why does he allow the rise of despots? The answer, of course, is that there isn't a good answer—not one that satisfies those doing the suffering, anyway. Theodicies, explanations for the existence of evil from a theistic perspective, are almost always inadequate, because the question of suffering cuts to the quick of faith. A deity who is all-powerful and all-good is a deity who should be able to prevent suffering. A deity who knows all should *know* it's happening, and should be able to do anything to stop such injustices. Yet, the suffering persists. It can be argued that abortion is simply one more terrible manifestation of the world's suffering and perhaps a matter of personal choice, but I still don't believe that God exists.

Is there any historical evidence to support the existence of St. Paul? What is your opinion on the theory that he may not have existed? THE HISTORICAL ST. PAUL by Michael R. Burch As every scholar with even a cursory knowledge of ancient history knows, there are two basic sources of information regarding the life of St. Paul, who was originally known as Saul of Tarsus. The first source is the set of epistles attributed to Paul, the thirteen books of the New Testament that bear his name. The second source is the Book of Acts, which is also a book within the New Testament. However, the Book of Acts and the Pauline epistles differ in significant ways regarding St. Paul’s life. Also problematic is the dating of all the original texts. However, there is ample historical attestation to the existence of “Paul,” at least. Let me explain. In the ancient world, many letters and pseudepigrapha (writings falsely attributed to someone) were written in the names of well-known, highly regarded historical figures. For example, an entire body of literature was once falsely attributed to the Greek philosopher Plato, including Plato's Republic. Many of the letters and pseudepigrapha came to have canonical status in the Bible. Although, in 451 AD, the Council of Chalcedon declared certain letters to be “apocryphal." (Apocrypha means “hidden things.”) And as almost every scholar agrees, neither the authenticity nor the dating of the original texts can be established with complete certitude. In other words, what we now see is not what was originally written. Much was lost or changed, or changed and lost. The most important writings of Paul are the seven authentic epistles: Romans, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Philippians, 1 Thessalonians, and Philemon. Although all thirteen letters, and all of the books of the New Testament, were carefully vetted. The reason for these doubts: Paul apparently wrote his epistles. However, as with the other books of the New Testament, the authenticity of the Pauline epistles is challenged by many biblical scholars. They were not copied directly by Paul’s own hand, but by scribes. I, like almost every scholar, find it beyond belief that all these men were lying, conspiring to perpetuate a hoax. By way of further support for the existence of St. Paul, it appears historians also did not doubt that St. Paul the Apostle's ministry was indeed a historical fact, however much they may debate the finer points of the details. If that is true, a consensus view, then why is the issue of his existence even raised?

What does John 14:14 mean? The interpretation of John 14:14 has been argued by theologians for centuries. It reads, “If you ask anything in my name, I will do it.” The key phrase is “in my name.” What, exactly, does that mean? Does it mean that we can get anything we want if we just tack “in Jesus’ name, amen” onto the end of our daily prayers? Most theologians, including myself, would say “no,” and would instead point to a contextual understanding of the passage. It means that those who ask “in Jesus’ name” act in accordance with his teachings. Because of these teachings, they embrace the life he lived, and live the life he commanded, a life, not of selfishness, but of selflessness, of sacrifice, of helping others, and of loving all humankind as God himself does. It also means that the supplicant acknowledges the sovereignty of Christ. This passage is linked to 1 John 5:14–15: “And this is the confidence which we have before Him, that, if we ask anything according to His will, He hears us. And if we know that He hears us in whatever we ask, we know that we have the requests which we have asked from Him.” Thus, if our prayers are aligned with God’s will—if our actions emulate Christ’s—the promised words apply. If, instead, our prayers are self-serving, vengeful, or simply not altruistic enough—if we merely wish for the suffering of our enemies, or great wealth or fame—we can’t very well expect to be heard, and our requests will remain unfulfilled.

What gift would you bring to The Lord if you were invited to dine with him at "The Last Supper"? A bouquet of my finest sonnets, bound in vellum and tied with silk no less exquisite than He deserves. Or, perhaps, a song—one of my own compositions, a hymn of gratitude for the gift of existence in this bewildering world. Perhaps, a perfect offering would be a silence as deep as the void, a state of utter presence, untainted by any plea.

Could you explain the Trinity from the Bible? The basic concept of the Trinity is that God is one, yet exists simultaneously in three coequal, coeternal, and consubstantial persons: the Father, the Son (Jesus Christ), and the Holy Spirit. The doctrine attempts to reconcile the Old Testament's concept of one God with the New Testament's revelations of Jesus as divine and the Holy Spirit as the "Spirit of God." Evidence cited in support of the Trinity includes: Jesus' claims of divinity and his acceptance of worship, the Holy Spirit’s role as a divine entity, and various biblical passages such as Matthew 28:19 ("Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit..."). The exact relationship between the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is a mystery, often described using analogies (such as water existing as ice, liquid, and vapor, or a three-leaf clover), but analogies always fall short.

Besides Athena, who was considered the most powerful goddess among the Greek gods? Besides Athena, who was considered the most powerful goddess among the Greek gods? It would have to be Hera, the wife of Zeus and queen of the gods. Zeus was, of course, the king. But Hera was the queen, and the Greeks seemed to have felt that power was shared at an almost equal level. She certainly had the power to make life difficult for Zeus’s paramours, who were many. One of them was Leto, who was pregnant. Hera was furious, and refused to allow Leto to give birth on any land that saw the sun. Finally, Leto gave birth in Delos, a floating island that didn’t exist until after Leto actually requested that it appear! Another problem that Hera had with Zeus was his fondness for Hercules, whom she tried to kill repeatedly. I would bet that if Hera had the same power as Zeus, she would have used it to kill him. Not even the immortal gods would have been safe.

If God asks you on Judgement Day, “Why didn't you believe in me,” what would you say to him? If God asks me, “Why not?” I would probably say something like, “I did not see sufficient evidence; I could not unsee what I saw, and I saw too much barbarity. You did not reveal yourself sufficiently, in a manner that led others to change their lives, their thoughts, their feelings, and their actions. Your book is a mess, a jumble of disjointed pronouncements and contradictory commands. You give us free will, then punish us for what we will, if we will the things you do not will, not just once, but for all eternity. You claim to love us, yet your love is capricious, arbitrary, and often cruel. You are more like a tyrannical dictator than a benevolent, understanding parent. Moreover, your supposed plan seems ill-conceived and full of errors. The entire cosmos is a cosmic fluke.” I understand that my answers would not be well-received, but the truth is most important.

What’s the most psychedelic poem, prose, or writing you’ve read or written? What’s the most psychedelic poem, prose, or writing you’ve read or written? For me, that’s a simple question. The most psychedelic piece of writing I’ve ever encountered is “The Inferno” by Dante Alighieri, particularly the sections detailing the various circles of Hell. The sheer scope of imagination, the nightmarish imagery, the visceral descriptions of torment and transformation, the sheer audacity to place real people in Hell, and the allegorical depth … all of it is so hallucinatory that it leaves me reeling and questioning reality even after multiple readings. The descriptions of the contrapasso—where the punishment fits the crime—are particularly striking. These moments are not mere descriptions; they are experiences. I've tried to write psychedelic poems myself, and those poems have been selected for publication by journals worldwide, but the result is a pale imitation when compared to Dante's Inferno. Dante's work doesn't just describe a hallucinatory world; it transports you there. I would not be surprised if the writing itself had a hallucinatory effect upon Dante, as well. Published by The Lyric, The Neovictorian/Cochlea, Rogue Scholars, Romantics Quarterly, Mindful of Poetry, Famous Poets and Poems, Poetry Life & Times, Other Voices International

Should Trump withdraw from being the Republican presidential nominee because he is too old and corrupt? It depends. If we are speaking hypothetically, if I were a Republican, my answer would, invariably, be a resounding "No!" But should I speak as a non-partisan independent, I'd suggest we're facing a Hobson's choice: a man in his late seventies, dogged by a host of legal entanglements, against a man approaching his ninth decade, whose public appeal now appears to be waning. The Republicans have a host of young, vigorous candidates, who might have a better chance. But will the electorate embrace them over Trump? One can only hope that sanity will prevail. The choice will most probably be Trump's to make. We shall see …

What are some great books to learn poetry, especially as a beginner? Great query! For beginners, I'd heartily recommend *How to Read a Poem: And Fall in Love with Poetry* by Edward Hirsch. It’s a marvelously accessible primer. For a more historical survey, consider *The Making of a Poem* edited by Eavan Boland and Mark Strand or Billy Collins’s *Poems of Our Moment*. If you're keen on form, which every aspiring wordsmith should be, explore *The Ode Less Traveled: Rhyme and Meter and What They Mean* by Stephen Fry, even though, like all books on poetry, it offers more opinions than certainties. Another worthy selection is *The Practice of Poetry* edited by Robin Beeman and Susan Swartwout. It is a solid collection that, besides offering an anthology, offers a number of insightful discussions.

How long will it take Bartolo Colon to get to the Baseball Hall of Fame in Cooperstown, New York? The answer is almost certainly never. Bartolo Colon’s numbers are not Hall of Fame worthy, although his longevity is to be admired. There are several key metrics that one would use to assess whether a player is potentially Hall of Fame-worthy. The first metric is wins above replacement, or WAR. The second metric is career wins, and wins in a season. Colon’s career numbers are okay but pale in comparison to Hall of Famers. Colon won 247 games during his career, which is a pretty good number. However, Hall of Fame pitchers such as Greg Maddux and Tom Glavine both won over 300 games. Colon does have a decent WAR number of 43.6, which is about average for Hall of Fame pitchers, but not great. Colon’s best seasons were obviously not as great as those of the Hall of Fame pitchers. He had a career 127 ERA+. His best season was 160 ERA+ which is very good, but not at the level of elite pitchers such as Maddux and Glavine. In conclusion, Colon was a solid pitcher. He would probably be given his own room in the Baseball Hall of Pretty Good.

How humane must William Shakespeare have been to cover so many things that mattered in his time? Must Shakespeare have been a humane soul, to encapsulate so many of his era’s concerns, from the highest aspirations of the noble class to the lowliest whispers in the taverns? Did he, too, wrestle with the questions that plague us still: Is it better to suffer the slings and arrows of outrageous fortune, or to take arms against a sea of troubles? Can a man truly be in love and yet be jealous, as the Moor of Venice so tragically proves? Was there in him, too, a wellspring of sorrow, a deep-seated melancholy that could transform itself into the most effervescent wit? Or was he simply a keen observer, a recorder of humanity’s foibles and passions, capable of slipping into the skin of kings and clowns with equal dexterity? Perhaps history can never truly know, but the plays themselves give an enduring glimpse of a heart that could break at the injustices of the world and soar with the glorious heights of love.

Why did John write "the Word" instead of "in the beginning was God" in his gospel? Is there any significance to this difference? The opening verses of the Gospel of John make those in Genesis seem a pale echo, a mere prelude to the Logos, the Word incarnate. The significance of “the Word” versus “God” is immense: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” No mere utterance, this Word which was God is the creative force, the divine essence, the very identity of the eternal. While the Genesis account establishes God at the beginning, John asserts that the Word *was already* there, co-existent with God, and *was* God. This is a profound theological statement, a declaration of the divinity of Jesus. It sets the stage for the entire gospel, emphasizing Jesus’ role not just as a prophet or teacher, but as the embodiment of God. The shift from a remote, creating God in Genesis to the active, immanent Word with God is a deliberate move to emphasize God's intimate relationship with humanity. By the phrase “The Word was with God” John points to this divine intimacy, and the final clause, “and the Word was God,” seals the deal, establishing the doctrine of the Trinity from page one. In this grand, opening assertion John has created a portrait of a God who is not only present in creation, but a God who is present in the creation's very essence.

When Trump turns on JD Vance (perhaps a scenario of the latter refusing to help Trump stage a coup after unfavorable election results, or some similar disloyalty), what do you predict will be Trump's nickname for him? A similar disloyalty is possible. My prediction? Trump will dub him "Jaded Vance," a snide encapsulation of his perceived betrayal, or perhaps "Quitting Vance,” a derisive jab at his supposed lack of grit, or maybe, just to keep it interesting, he'll unleash a full-blown series of pejoratives, which will then be repeated ad nauseam by his most rabid fans, until the names, the barbs, the taunts, become the accepted truth in their fevered minds. Or perhaps there will be a single, perfect sobriquet, designed to sting the most profoundly. “Traitor Vance,” reflecting Trump’s unwavering sense of victimhood and the perceived crimes against him. Given Trump’s penchant for playground taunts and his lack of imagination, it’s anyone’s guess. The possibilities are as varied as they are vulgar.

Could Prime Shaq defend Jokic? Absolutely not! The thought experiment is fascinating, though, as both behemoths are historical dominators. Prime Shaquille O’Neal was a force of nature—nearly unstoppable near the basket with his size, strength, and surprising agility. Nikola Jokic, on the other hand, is a basketball maestro, a virtuoso of passing, shooting, and court awareness. While Shaq could likely bully Jokic on the ground and make scoring tough, Jokic’s strategic brilliance and outside shooting would likely exploit Shaq’s weaknesses on the perimeter. Shaq would have his share of offensive success and points, I’m fairly certain, but as the game went on, Jokic would likely outmaneuver and ultimately, outscore him and his team. It's like a chess match with a sledgehammer—brutal power versus exquisite skill. Jokic would definitely win the chess match. What makes it even a more interesting question is considering a hypothetical team. What an epic battle!

What is the meaning of 1 Corinthians 13? It is the loveliest chapter in the Bible, and one of the most misused. Paul’s meditation on agape has been misinterpreted, misapplied and generally mauled by the religiously inclined. The most common misunderstanding concerns the meaning of “love.” The “love” of 1 Corinthians 13 has nothing to do with romantic love, or even the love of a parent for a child. It refers to the selfless benevolence often described as “God’s Love.” This is a tough love which offers correction when needed, and demands, above all, loyalty to the divine word. Love is patient and kind; love does not envy or boast; it is not arrogant or rude. It does not insist on its own way; it is not irritable or resentful; it does not rejoice at wrongdoing, but rejoices with the truth. Love bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. Love never ends. If there are prophecies, they will pass away; if there are tongues, they will cease; if there is knowledge, it will pass away. For we know in part and we prophesy in part, but when the perfect comes, the partial will pass away. When I was a child, I spoke like a child, I thought like a child, I reasoned like a child. When I became a man, I gave up childish ways. For now we see in a mirror dimly, but then face to face. Now I know in part; then I shall know fully, even as I have been fully known. So now faith, hope, and love abide, these three; but the greatest of these is love. This passage is often read aloud during weddings, but it has nothing whatsoever to do with romantic relationships. In the ancient Greek, there are three words for “love,” one being eros, our “erotic love,” another being philia, or the platonic bond between friends or family members, and agape, the all-encompassing love of God. 1 Corinthians 13 speaks of agape. As the preeminent scholar of the ancient Greek language has written: “In ancient Greece, the word agape was not used until the first century, and it was used almost exclusively to describe God’s love for man!” Now, what this has to do with weddings, I can only guess. But it has everything to do with the relationship between believer and Deity. When misused in this way, the passage becomes a shallow platitude, a feel-good confection, and a betrayal of the divine word. In the end, it becomes meaningless.

Why did God punish the mortal serpent instead of the devil for deceiving Eve? Because according to the Jewish/Christian account in Genesis, the serpent *was* the devil, masquerading as a helpful creature to entice Eve to abandon her faith and trust in God. The Bible does not explicitly identify the serpent as Satan, but this is the common interpretation, supported by verses in the Book of Revelation. Thus, in punishing the serpent, God was also punishing Satan, the tempter. There's a second interesting point. God didn’t punish Eve directly, either. He punished her for succumbing to temptation: to eat the forbidden fruit from the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil. This punishment also included a series of curses upon her descendants. But the serpent was a tool and was punished just for that. God is often portrayed as a benevolent being in contrast to this version in Genesis, which is difficult to deal with unless we see that what is being portrayed is perhaps some combination of reality and allegory. Why the serpent and not Satan immediately? Perhaps because the allegory works best if we see the origin of evil as something less personal: more like the actions of a single being. And if it begins in a garden, temptation can have a certain “natural” appeal that might resonate with the original writers. The story can, thus, easily be framed without directly using the name Satan. The reader is given a clue, and is meant to figure out — or to not to figure it out, and accept things on faith. In the end, the real reason for the punishment of the serpent may be that the serpent was perceived as the instrument of the Fall, and, as such, a key player in the drama of sin and redemption.

Do you think in the future Oleksandr Usyk will share the title of the greatest fighter of all time with Muhammad Ali? With the caveat that it's all subjective, the answer is probably no. Muhammad Ali transcended boxing, and Usyk, while an undeniably gifted champion, operates in a different stratum, one of incredible boxing ability, but lacking the charisma, the political sway, the artistic impact, and the universal recognition that made Ali a global icon. Ali’s impact went far beyond the ring; he was a cultural force, a symbol of resistance, defiance, and self-belief. His name is known throughout the world; for countless people, he *is* boxing. Usyk, on the other hand, is, and will likely remain, a superb boxer, a technical master with a granite chin, but his star hasn't, and likely won’t, reach the same supernova level. While Usyk's accomplishments are extraordinary, and he could conceivably be ranked among the top ten fighters in history, comparing him to Ali feels like comparing apples and, well, a supernova.

Why was Jesus also praying to God when the trinity knows that he is also God? That’s quite a philosophical conundrum, isn’t it? The Trinity, this divine triad of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, presents a mind-bending paradox, a sacred mystery to be pondered and accepted rather than dissected and understood with mortal instruments. It’s like trying to grasp the infinity of space or the infinitesimal dance of subatomic particles—the deeper one delves, the more elusive the truth becomes. Why would Jesus, who *is* God, pray to God? Well, perhaps it highlights the human aspect of Jesus, his humility, his submission to the divine will. Or maybe it’s a demonstration, a lesson for humankind on the proper relationship with the Almighty. It’s a matter of faith, really, because even the most erudite theologians and philosophers stumble when trying to fully explain the inexplicable. Think of it like trying to capture the scent of a rose—you can analyze its chemical composition, describe its appearance, but you can’t quite convey the experience of inhaling its fragrance. The essence remains just beyond reach. It does boggle the mind, though.

What would Usyk need to do to get inside your top 10 all-time heavyweight list? USYK’S HEAVYWEIGHT MOVEMENT by Michael R. Burch  To break into any reasonable boxing aficionado’s top ten all-time heavyweight list, what would Oleksandr Usyk need to do? Quite a bit, actually. The Ukrainian is, quite obviously, a generational talent and a brilliant technician, but the heavyweight division has always been, and will forevermore be, about the “big boys.” The Ukrainian has already shown that a good big man can beat a good small man, but that only gets him a gold watch. His next few fights need to be stellar, not just wins, and he has to get his hands on some of those old-school sluggers (I’m looking at you, Tyson Fury), so the public can determine if “style” can beat sheer, brutal “power.” Usyk has the skills, the agility, and the footwork of a world-class welterweight, but is he tough enough to absorb a legitimate haymaker from, say, a young George Foreman? We don’t know yet because he hasn’t been tested that way. He has heart, but he needs to develop more whiskers. Has he ever heard the sound of his own eardrums vibrating? If he wants to sit at the high table, he has to take the hardest punches the division has to offer and keep standing. The men who were at the top, from Ali to Louis, were gladiators. They didn’t just win, they survived rounds of punishment that would cripple any but the truly stout. At 37 years old, Usyk has time, but not much. He may be running out of time, but not because he lacks talent or a will to win. He has a chance at history. But, to earn his spot, he must survive. His next few fights will tell the tale.

Why do people not believe in the writings in the Bible? Why don’t people believe what the Bible says? Why do people reject the sacred texts of the Bible? Do the words ring hollow, devoid of truth? For what reasons, what misgivings, lead so many to disbelieve the ancient prophecies and moral decrees? Is it a matter of faith? Logic? Or perhaps an aversion to the tales themselves?

After Jesus raised Lazarus from the dead and caused the blind to see, shouldn't such miracles be proof that He is the Messiah? After all, if Jesus was not the Messiah, wouldn't that mean He was a wizard or a charlatan? And why not? The Bible says: "He that believeth on him is not condemned: but he that believeth not is condemned already, because he hath not believed in the name of the only begotten Son of God. And this is the condemnation, that light is come into the world, and men loved darkness rather than light, because their deeds were evil. For every one that doeth evil hateth the light, neither cometh to the light, lest his deeds should be reproved.” (John 3:18-20) The question arises: if those are miracles performed not by a deity, how can we know if such miracles are evidence for the divinity of Jesus, since conjuring tricks and illusions had likely been performed frequently for many centuries or even millennia? What if Jesus was a superb illusionist or magician? Or what if he borrowed a few of his spectacular effects from the Egyptians, like the pyramids? The Apostle Paul would seem to take the position that our "faith" does not necessarily depend on "proof." Paul said: “Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen.” (Hebrews 11:1, KJV). Yet many insist otherwise. If one cannot see the "evidence" of the miracles, how can one believe? And what “evidence” is truly "beyond dispute?" When, historically, would an empirical test be reliable to authenticate miracles? Perhaps the only thing “beyond dispute” is that we all, sooner or later, die.

What are some of the most memorable moments in Tennessee sports history? The Big Orange: UT Vols’ 1998 National Championship. I’ll never forget that season, the passion, the grit, and the ultimate triumph against Florida State in the Fiesta Bowl. It was a culmination of years of striving, spearheaded by Peyton Manning's legacy and the masterful coaching of Phillip Fulmer, turning Knoxville into an absolute frenzy of celebration. The game was intensely competitive, and the victory signified not just a win for UT, but a statewide rallying point, uniting Vols fans in a shared moment of unadulterated glory. The atmosphere in Tennessee was electrified, and the celebrations went on for days. This was the pinnacle of college football for many, etching itself into the minds and the hearts of Volunteers fans both young and old. It remains a symbol of a time when everything in the sporting world felt within reach.

How does Larry Holmes’ legacy change if he never beat up an old Ali? What do you think? Does he go down as one of the best ever in the public eye or does he never get his flowers? LARRY HOLMES: UNDERRATED CHAMPION? by Michael R. Burch I've always felt Larry Holmes was underrated, and I think his legacy would be considerably more lustrous had he not been the man to administer the first defeat to Muhammad Ali. Although Ali was well beyond his prime, the fact remains that Ali, no matter how shopworn, was still Ali. And when Ali lost, the entire world grieved. One would have thought Holmes had committed an atrocity. The truth is, Holmes didn't exactly make them "eat their words," as he was an excellent boxer but he never approached the charisma of The Greatest. Perhaps the greatest tragedy associated with the Holmes-Ali fight for Holmes himself lies in the fact that Ali, no matter how diminished, would remain a more popular figure with the global boxing community, his legend practically inviolable. In the end, by defeating Ali, Holmes gained very little beyond the victory, but lost considerably in terms of his reputation. And there is the irony. Holmes’ career was one of the best by any standard, but his victory over Ali somehow detracted and diminished it. Holmes beat virtually everyone put in front of him. Holmes may be the most underrated heavyweight champion ever because the public never really gave him the credit he was due. He did whatever he had to do, and did it well. The man was a terrific fighter, and the only man of his era who could claim to have been better than Holmes, arguably, was Mike Tyson, and maybe a few others, who often ducked and dodged Holmes. With that in mind, had Holmes never fought Ali, perhaps his achievements would be seen in an even more favorable and less tainted light. Ironically, as a result of having beaten a legend, most casual boxing fans will probably continue to view Holmes’ great career as something less than it was.
Can anyone or anything overthrow your belief in the Jewish God? No.

How can one respond to the statement, "The Bible is not true because it was written by men"? It’s hardly an airtight rejoinder, yet there is a certain undeniable tautology to the claim that the Bible, a tome composed by mortal scribes, is therefore bereft of eternal truth. However, to my way of thinking, the crux of the matter lies not in the authorship but in the veracity of the claims within. To retort with any degree of cogency, one must first establish the existence of other religious texts and then compare these books to the Bible: is there a similar claim against the Qu’ran, the Bhagavad Gita, or the Book of Mormon, for that matter? Is it reasonable, then, to suggest that *all* religious texts are therefore untrue simply because their genesis lies in human hands—as if divinity chose only to etch its precepts into the stone of a mountain or a burning bush? Perhaps it’s worth noting that those who penned the Bible were, at least ostensibly, inspired, even moved. And in some instances, these authors claimed direct encounters with the divine. Then the matter becomes not of authorship, but of credibility: do the tenets within the Bible reflect a higher truth, and do the alleged miracles seem plausible to you?

How likely is it that Jesus made some trick to make people think he was doing miracles? Miracles, magic, and the Almighty are all pretty much the same thing: an attempt to bend the laws of physics—or, more accurately, an attempt to get someone to believe in the bending of the “laws of physics.” Perhaps Jesus had the charisma of a cult leader, and, as with many cult leaders, he understood that dramatic demonstrations are extremely persuasive, and what is most likely is he took advantage of the credulous people he was speaking to. With or without trickery, it's the effect of their belief that changed lives. After all, a good magician doesn’t reveal his illusions. When it comes to faith, how likely is it that *we* would not be influenced by our desires, fears, and the ever-present human capacity for self-deception—and how likely is a true religion to be based on these things?

In your opinion, what is the most overrated solution to a problem? The word "solution" implies that there is a problem, so I'd have to say, the notion that "money can solve everything." Money is certainly helpful, but it often masks the underlying issues, like placing a shiny veneer over a crumbling edifice. It can provide temporary relief, a placebo perhaps, but it rarely addresses the root cause of the malady. Think of the well-intentioned but often misguided philanthropic efforts, which, while generating publicity and occasionally providing a few creature comforts, fail to eradicate systemic problems. A truly sustainable approach, I believe, requires more than a simple injection of capital; it mandates a complete overhaul of the underlying structures, the systems engendering the inequities. The belief that throwing money at a problem equates to its resolution is not only overrated, but it's also, often, a dangerous delusion.

What do you think will happen to José Abreu in the MLB after being released by the Houston Astros? I am unable to prognosticate the future with any kind of certainty, but I can tell you this: José Abreu’s release from the Houston Astros—a team for which he was woefully under-performing—signals a sharp downturn for the once-celebrated slugger. His career arc is following the same trajectory as so many other aging players: talent diminishes, skills erode, and the ball seems to go precisely where the fielder is positioned. The Astros’ decision makes perfect economic sense. With Abreu’s salary no longer on the books, the team will have more financial flexibility to make a deal for a superior player. However, don’t expect Abreu to simply vanish; he will likely find his way onto another team that is willing to take a gamble, hoping that he can recapture some of his former glory. But, in my view, he’s past his prime. His reflexes are a bit slower. His swing isn’t so fierce. And I doubt we’ll see him deliver again.

Who is better, Wilt or Magic? Wilt Chamberlain was a physical marvel, a human skyscraper with a skillset that boggled the mind. But Magic Johnson was a maestro, a conductor of chaos, who wove his teammates into a symphony of victory. Wilt’s dominance was undeniable, yet Magic’s impact transcended mere statistics; he was the heartbeat of a dynasty, the smiling face of basketball’s golden era. Both changed the game, but in distinct ways. Wilt’s force flattened opponents, while Magic elevated them, empowering them to achieve their best selves. He brought a joy to the court that Wilt, hampered by dourness, never quite achieved. And so, while Wilt might be statistically dominant, Magic’s all-around influence is the greater. He made the game beautiful.

Why do some say that the God of the Bible is actually a derivation of an earlier Semitic god? THE ORIGINAL FIRE GODS by Michael R. Burch  It has long been suggested that Yahweh, the so-called "God of the Bible," is a derivation of the Canaanite god El, who was frequently depicted as a fire god, as were many of the most important gods and goddesses of the ancient world. If a certain god or goddess was portrayed as a fire god, it meant that it was associated with transformative power, with destruction as well as creation. Even the ancient Greek god of the forge and volcanoes, Hephaestus, was a fire god, frequently shown in the company of fire-breathing Cyclops and the most terrifying weapons. Fire was also associated with the sun and with the divine spark of life. As the author Daniel A. Siedell noted, "fire is a primal force, and the fire god or goddess is thus, like the other major deities, a universal figure." El was the father of the ancient Canaanite gods, and he was also a creator god and the god of wisdom and knowledge. In the early days of Yahwism there was a feminine aspect often added to his name—Yahweh and his Asherah—with Yahweh and Asherah being worshiped together in a single temple that could be found in Israel, dating back to possibly 1000 BC. Then, with the changes to Yahwism, the feminine aspect was dropped, to be later replaced by monotheism—with Yahweh being seen as a god that needed no other deities. It is, however, widely believed that the early Israelites and Jews took El and changed his name, replacing "El" with "Yahweh" in their prayers and hymns. Many scholars believe Yahweh was one of the most important gods in the early Canaanite pantheon, and that he was associated with storms, war, and conquest. So to answer the question, early Yahweh was often a fire god, just like El—and both El and Yahweh were associated with transformative power, destruction as well creation.

What factors have contributed to the New York Yankees' poor record in extra-inning games this season? The Yankees' recent struggles, particularly in added frames, are a vexing puzzle, but several interlocking elements appear to be at play. Firstly, a demonstrable lack of clutch hitting has plagued the team when the pressure ratchets up. Meaningful knocks with runners in scoring position simply haven't materialized with sufficient frequency, a deficiency that exacerbates any perceived shortcomings. Secondly, the bullpen, typically a bastion of strength for New York, has occasionally faltered, offering up costly runs and uncharacteristic meltdowns in crucial moments. Thirdly, strategic decisions made late in games, including bullpen usage and pinch-hitting choices, have, at times, backfired. In brief, a confluence of offensive drought, bullpen inconsistency, tactical errors, and perhaps a bit of simple bad luck, when these combined elements rear their collective heads, they become amplified, costing the Yankees several crucial wins.

How does professional boxer Floyd Mayweather Jr. compare to Muhammad Ali in terms of bravery? Boxers are, by definition, brave, so to compare any two elite fighters on this basis could seem superfluous—a pointless exercise in hyperbole. Courage, in the boxing arena, is a given. But perhaps the question isn’t about the existence of bravery; it's about the scale, the scope, and the *kind* of courage each man displayed. Ali's bravery wasn’t merely confined to the ring. His most significant, and, in many ways, bravest actions, occurred outside the ropes, during the throes of the Civil Rights Movement, when he refused induction into the military. That decision, made in the face of immense pressure, public condemnation, and the threat of imprisonment, was an act of tremendous courage, far exceeding anything he accomplished while fighting. Mayweather, on the other hand, for all his defensive brilliance and incredible success, has been a far more predictable figure. He has not had to make potentially career-ending decisions, nor has his persona been synonymous with political or social upheaval. Both men are, undeniably, brave, but their courage takes radically different forms, and perhaps, it is Ali's bravery that resonates with a deeper, more profound meaning for the ages.

What was Satan's role before becoming an adversary? Satan's role before his fall from grace — if we're to put stock in such antiquated narratives — was, it would seem, as a sort of celestial policeman, a cosmic enforcer. He was, according to some interpretations, the angel charged with keeping tabs on humanity, a celestial snoop charged with ferreting out any transgressions against the divine will. In a sense, he was God’s eyes and ears, reporting back on the peccadilloes and outright sins of humankind, acting as a celestial prosecuting attorney, if you will, bringing charges against the wayward and the wicked. This role, the role of a celestial informant, seems to have been a thankless one, a thankless but crucial task in God's grand design. It’s a role, one might argue, that placed him in a unique position where the temptation of pride and the seeds of rebellion could be most easily sown, as if he was destined for inevitable apostasy.

How different has this presidential election felt compared to last time? Does Trump have the same energy, momentum, and grassroots support? Have you noticed people turning on Trump? The 2024 presidential campaign is shaping up to be a stark contrast to the 2020 election. Trump's rallies still draw large crowds, but the unbridled exuberance of the past seems somewhat muted, replaced by a more cautious mood. Many of Trump's core supporters remain steadfast, but some, jaded by past disappointments and controversies, are quietly drifting away. The enthusiasm isn't quite the same, and the rallies, though still sizable, lack the frenetic energy of those earlier campaigns. The shifts in voter sentiment are subtle, often conveyed in quiet conversations rather than boisterous pronouncements, yet are certainly palpable. One gets the distinct impression that more people are now questioning their support, or at least, are viewing the landscape with increased skepticism. I also wonder, is this campaign a rerun, or is it a whole new show?

Why shouldn't kobe be put in the same level as MJ and LeBron James? Kobe Bryant was a truly transcendent basketball player, yes, but his statistics still fell short of both Michael Jordan’s and LeBron James’. Bryant’s scoring average was lower, his field goal percentage weaker, his assists less frequent, and his rebounds fewer. While he does have the advantage of two more Finals appearances than James, his Finals winning percentage is lower, and James’ triple-double numbers exceed Bryant’s by a wide margin. Jordan’s career statistics are simply beyond compare. His playoff performances, and his Finals statistics, were also more consistent. Bryant was also a notoriously poor passer. It's a tough argument. And yet, Bryant’s killer instinct, his tenacious defense, his clutch shooting, and his unwavering dedication to the game, are all without peer. He also won an Oscar. And his influence on the game is still being felt today. So, while statistical comparisons may not fully capture his impact, Bryant’s legacy, like that of Jordan and James, is now etched in the pantheon of basketball legends. It is undeniable.

If evolution is proven to be a fact, what happens to the Bible and the stories of creation? IF evolution were to be definitively established as an incontrovertible fact, the inevitable consequence would be a profound re-evaluation of the stories of creation as presented in the Bible, and by extension, the scriptures of all fundamentalist religions. The Genesis creation account would immediately be demoted to the realm of literary metaphor. Its literal interpretation, so cherished by many, could no longer be sustained, even if one sought to interpret its seemingly impossible accounts. The narrative of a six-day creation, the formation of humankind from dust, the existence of a single, original couple, and the subsequent descent into sin—all of these notions would be irreconcilably challenged, and it would have an awful effect on belief. Faced with scientifically validated evidence of a long-standing evolutionary process, the fundamental tenets of the Genesis narrative would inevitably be subjected to critical scrutiny. The need to reconcile these two opposing viewpoints would then be crucial.

Why are Americans stuck with Biden and Trump? The American political landscape, a curious tapestry woven from threads of circumstance, apathy, and, perhaps, a perverse sense of dramatic irony, often leaves observers scratching their heads. We find ourselves, once again, with a choice that, for many, feels less like an opportunity and more like a preordained path, a well-trodden route with familiar signposts and predictable detours. The reasons for this perceived predicament are as multifold as the faces in a crowded caucus, as varied as the opinions aired on cable news. One could point to the inherent inertia of established political systems, where the levers of power, once grasped, are loath to loosen their grip. Or, perhaps, we are the unwitting pawns of a carefully orchestrated game, expertly played by unseen hands that benefit from our stagnation. The American electorate, a vast, diverse, and often fractious entity, is not a monolith. Its preferences, ideologies, and priorities are as divergent as its geographical spread. This inherent complexity makes the task of forging a truly unifying consensus all but impossible, leaving the field open to those who can best exploit our divisions, the skilled rhetoricians and masterful manipulators who can tap into our fears, anxieties, and aspirations. The media landscape has metamorphosed into a series of echo chambers, each reinforcing pre-existing biases and limiting exposure to alternative viewpoints which, in turn, fosters polarization. It’s also possible, of course, that we are being misled to believe there's a problem, when, in fact, the whole situation is merely the way things are.

Can you explain the difference between the terms 'Satan' and 'Devil'? Satan is an individual, a specific entity, a character. The Devil is a title, a descriptive term that can be applied to varying figures or used to describe a general force of evil. Satan is often depicted as a fallen angel, a rebel against God, and the embodiment of temptation and sin. The term ‘devil’ is more generic and can refer to any agent or manifestation of wickedness, mischief, or destruction. Both words are often used interchangeably, to a certain degree, although the nuance does shift, depending on the context, and the beliefs of the person using the terms. For example, in the Christian tradition, the Devil is sometimes described as a tempter, a deceiver, but the same characteristics apply to Satan. There are various interpretations of each term found in different religious and philosophical traditions, although each is primarily used in Western culture.

What is your favorite book/chapter/verse in the Bible? Why do you like it? My favorite book of the Bible is, perhaps predictably, Ecclesiastes. The melancholy beauty of its lamentations—the sighing breath of “vanity, vanity, all is vanity”—resonates with a depth of feeling that transcends its apparent pessimism. I find a strange solace in its unwavering acknowledgement of the transience and ultimate meaninglessness of earthly endeavors. The author's grappling with faith, doubt, and the inescapable approach of death, all in elegantly phrased, often paradoxical, language, speaks to my own wrestling with the mysteries of existence. I am particularly fond of the third chapter— “To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven.” It offers a framework of understanding, even as it acknowledges the cycles of human experience. Perhaps the comfort inherent in this acknowledgement is itself a testament to something, a way of finding the sacred in the mundane. The wisdom of Ecclesiastes is timeless, a testament to the human condition. It is the most honest book in a book of dubious honesty.

What poem would you teach your child? I'd teach her "The Raven," of course, by Edgar Allan Poe. That poem is so unforgettable because it captures the darkness, the mystery, the longing, the pain, the relentless, gnawing sorrow, so well. I've never been able to read "The Raven" without crying, and I never want to be able to read it without crying. But, of course, for a young child, "The Raven" might be a bit too dark. So I'd start with something gentler, "The Tyger" by William Blake, or "The Lamb." Or perhaps a few lines from "Ozymandias" by Percy Bysshe Shelley, though that one, too, is probably a bit beyond her age. The key there is to plant the seed. I would also teach her my poem, "At Wilfred Owen's Grave," but I'd have to choose the parts, and make sure she understood it, so again, maybe one day. I might also read her "If" by Rudyard Kipling, one that everyone should know since it gets to the heart of nobility and grace, despite its Victorian-era stiffness. And if I could, I'd have to read it to her with the voice of her grandfather who has passed on, because he read it to me when I was that age. I can still remember every inflection of his voice. But mostly, I think, I'd try to teach her poetry by example. Reading her poetry every day, for example. Being a poet, herself. Showing her the power of language, and love.

How do the Jews explain all of the Old Testament prophecies that Jesus fulfilled? Do they edit those prophecies out of their bibles? Jews have a different interpretation of the Old Testament than Christians. They do not edit the prophecies out of their bibles, but they interpret them differently. For example, Christians believe certain prophecies foretold the coming of Jesus Christ, and the fulfillment of those prophecies are proof that he was the Messiah. Jews, however, understand these prophecies as referring to Jewish figures or events, or as general statements about the future. They do not accept the Christian interpretation of these prophecies, nor do they believe Jesus was the promised Messiah.

Why isn’t George Sisler mentioned more as one of the best players to ever play baseball? GEORGE SISLER: THE UNFORGETTABLE NAME IN BASEBALL by Michael R. Burch There are many forgotten names in the baseball pantheon, but some, like George Sisler, are more deserving of a prominent place in the baseball history books. Sisler played from 1915-1930, missing one year due to World War I and 1923 due to sinusitis that severely impaired his vision. His lifetime batting average of .340 is the highest of any player whose career began in the twentieth century. His 2,810 career hits were good enough for fifth all-time when he retired, even though his career was severely shortened by those two unfortunate events. Had he played even two more seasons, those hits might have been enough to put him atop the list, though some of his contemporaries played many more seasons. His 257 career stolen bases are also a testament to a speed that would have been exceptional in any era.
