He was a dominant hitter at a time when dominant hitters had to face the best pitching in baseball. He led the American League in hits twice, in stolen bases four times and in batting average twice. His career has been obscured by the unfortunate events of his career. He may not have been quite as famous as some of the other greats, but in his prime, he was as good as any player of any era. Had he not been a great player, he would probably have been able to take over a team as manager. So I’ve always wondered, why Sisler isn’t mentioned more as one of the game’s all-time best?

Do you think Jake Paul will be remembered as a legitimate boxer in the future? Jake Paul, the YouTube star turned pugilist, seems to have mastered the art of generating both outrage and attention, which is the very lifeblood of the modern entertainment complex. Whether he'll be "remembered" as a *legitimate* boxer, however, is an entirely different matter. The world of boxing, as a rule, is a merciless meritocracy—even for men who are not remotely men. While Paul has shown flashes of athleticism and punching power, the level of competition he has faced to date has been, frankly, laughable. If he continues to hand-pick his opponents like a spoiled child selecting his favorite candy from a vast, all-you-can-eat buffet, it is hard to see his legacy lasting a season, much less a lifetime. But if he dares to step into the ring with a bona fide contender, then perhaps his story might be different. Then, and only then, might future boxing aficionados actually mention his name with, if not reverence, then at least a grudging respect. For now, however, he remains a curious sideshow, not yet ready for the main tent.

Have dragons or sea serpents ever been seen in the world? If so, why haven't they been captured? Sea serpents, such as the ones described in the *Physiologus,* have intrigued mariners and landlubbers alike for millennia. The notion of behemoths residing in the deepest recesses of the ocean's inky depths, creatures whose scales shimmer with an eldritch gleam and whose serpentine forms could swallow whole ships, has spurred countless voyages of exploration, as well as lurid tall tales, and equally lurid, albeit inaccurate, depictions in bestiaries. Dragons, too, have captured the popular imagination, though typically they’re relegated to the terrestrial realm—though some are said to be aquatic as well. Why haven’t these creatures been captured, if they are in fact real? There’s no proof, despite persistent reports, that dragons or sea serpents exist in the world. It's not a question of them eluding capture; it’s more a matter of them not being real. It is far more straightforward, and certainly quicker, to dispatch the notion that these creatures might exist by simply dismissing them as fantasy. If they were real, it would be difficult for them to remain undetected, given today’s technologies. Even centuries ago, it would have been quite difficult for a massive creature to go unnoticed by humans, even with the limited technology of the time. But we have a far greater understanding of the world than did our ancestors, and it's unlikely that such formidable creatures remain unknown.

Can you provide some examples of short poems with a rhyme scheme? **Short Rhymed Poems** by Michael R. Burch The sun descends; the day is done— A golden gleam, a setting sun! And though it wearies, come what may, There’s naught but dusk and night—and stay!  The wind sighed low, a mournful sound, As dead leaves drifted to the ground. And I beheld the weeping trees rustle in the breeze.  The fireflies dance on fragrant breeze, among the tall and ancient trees, and I and you, we share the night, by dancing in firelight.  The sun slips down to silent sea. Remember her? As did I. This memory, I see it plain. Yet I shall meet her never again.  Love is a wild and splendid thing, a song the nightingales sing. But you have gone, and I am left bereft!

What's the name of your church, and what attracts you in there? It seems the name of my particular, peculiar chapel would be the Free Thinkers’ Sanctuary for the Cynical and Curious—a mouthful, I confess. What draws me? The utter lack of dogma, for openers. No required genuflection, no fearmongering, no stained-glass windows depicting the grotesque, apocryphal antics of long-dead zealots. Instead, we have dusty tomes, the scent of aged paper and leather, sunlight streaming through the high, unadorned panes, and the quiet murmur of contemplation, of grappling with the unanswerable. Intellect is the altar, skepticism the incense, and literature the liturgy, if you will. It's a place where questions are not only welcomed but cherished, where doubt is not a sin but a sacred duty. We worship at the shrine of the unknown, acknowledging the vastness of that which we do not, and perhaps cannot, comprehend. What draws me? The freedom to be wrong, to explore the cosmos within and without, and the solace found in the company of fellow travelers on this bewildering odyssey we call life.

What relationship do you have with Satan? The author is most certainly not a Satanist, nor would he want to be. One might as well ask what relationship he has with the Bogeyman or Freddy Krueger. He much prefers the Cookie Monster, the Tooth Fairy or Tinkerbell. He would never join a cult that promotes or glorifies inhumanity. He is not "tempted" by either the carrot or the stick. He would not sacrifice virtue, morals, love or beauty for some cheap parlor trick of "power" or "glory.” He holds that all things are better left undone than corrupted. He believes in the better angels of his nature, and those of us with a modicum of common sense. He does not require, nor does he seek, either damnation or salvation. Truth, beauty, and justice are what matter. He would not consort, in any respect, with such darkness.

I recently purchased my copy of the President Trump endorsed “God Bless the USA” Bible. Isn’t it wonderful how Trump is encouraging our country to turn back to God and pray daily? I also obtained a copy of this auspicious volume. It warms my heart to see the confluence of faith and patriotism, the yearning for a return to the moral compass that once guided our nation. In the face of a world seemingly adrift from its moorings, this initiative strikes me as a timely and vital one. The very essence of our liberties and the very fabric of our society have always been inextricably tied to a shared devotion to the Almighty. I have always loved hearing the music of Lee Greenwood. And what could be more American than our national anthem? A return to such touchstones, a rekindling of the flame of divine guidance, is precisely what our nation needs.

Would you describe Trump as Evil Incarnate? I am not certain whether Donald Trump is "evil incarnate," although I do believe, as the Greeks asserted, that "the road to hell is paved with good intentions," and Trump has certainly paved that road in many ways, especially in regard to environmental issues, as he had a near-pathological aversion to all things green. I suppose that could be considered evil, but I’m just not sure I am capable of taking a position so absolutist, since I know that there is something of good and evil in all of us, and what a few perceive as evil, others see as good depending on their perspective. The problem with describing someone as “evil incarnate” is it shuts off, or at least slows, debate and argument which is what one should be striving for, rather than just putting a label on someone and dismissing them. The real question is: is Trump more evil than the average politician? Is he more evil than most people in general? Is he far more evil than most U.S. presidents? And those questions have no easy answers.

How was Mike Tyson generally ranked "all-time" between 1988 and 1991? Was there already a perception that Mike Tyson might be a top 5 heavyweight ever between those years (and between ages 21 and 24)? Mike Tyson was generally ranked as the #1 heavyweight boxer in the world between 1988 and 1991, which coincided roughly with his prime years, ages 21 to 24. Many boxing experts and fans held the view then that, if he kept winning, he would be considered one of the top five heavyweights of all time, possibly even number one. However, the potential of being great was constantly juxtaposed with the knowledge that his success depended on factors beyond the ring: discipline, focus, the lack of self-sabotage. His losses to Buster Douglas, followed by his conviction for rape, cemented the fact that his greatness, though perhaps undeniable, remained a “what might have been” scenario.

If Jews don't believe in Jesus, then why make the whole first half of the Bible about them? Some say it's to establish familial connections to the Messiah, but that’s questionable, since the Messiah also had to be God. Why would God, the First Cause, put so much effort into engineering a “family” for a son whom some believe to have been miraculously born, but not of a pre-existing family? And if God needs a family, why not just build one? Or better yet, why not just be born? Since God’s time does not exist, time would not have to have any impact on His eternal nature. And since we have to take the Bible on faith, is it not more reasonable to believe the Bible when it’s saying something—anything—that actually makes some sort of sense? Or doesn’t make us question an omnipotent, omniscient, omnipresent being’s questionable grasp of common sense? My faith is more than one big head-scratching session. When I finally encounter God, I want to have something more than a simple request for an explanation. Not that I expect to understand. I hope, at least, the Almighty is well-prepared for the questions of those who have spent their lives making some sense of things, and maybe have a few of their own.

What star player of the Negro League is thought to be able to challenge the major league but didn't? The player who is thought to have the ability to challenge the major league but didn’t is Satchel Paige. Despite his extraordinary talent, he was kept out of the major leagues until the age of 42, after the color barrier began to fall. Many baseball experts believe Paige might have been one of the greatest pitchers ever had he been allowed to showcase his abilities against major league competition during his prime. His exceptional curveball and fastball, along with his remarkable control, could have made him an unstoppable force. He also possessed an incredibly high baseball IQ and a dominating presence on the mound, characteristics that would have made him a formidable opponent for any batter. Yet, because of racial discrimination, Paige’s extraordinary skills were confined to the Negro Leagues for the majority of his career. He was a legend, a giant in his own right, but forced to perform in a separate, unequal world.

How was God born? “How was God born?” is, of course, an absurd question, since time and space did not exist before the supposed genesis of our universe. It’s like asking where the sound went after you turned off the volume of a song. I personally attribute this question to the ongoing, seemingly endless philosophical and theological discussions throughout the ages about the First Cause of the origin of the universe. The problem is that, as far as I know, there has been zero proof, zero convincing arguments, and zero agreement. So … who knows? God might be like the Cookie Monster, never born, always exists, always eating cookies. Or perhaps God is like the Tooth Fairy —she doesn’t exist, but is still fun, the giver of small tokens of grace, a sweet lie. Perhaps God is Tinker Bell, and you have to believe in her to keep her alive. Or perhaps God is like a joke that falls flat time after time, no matter how many angles you try to approach. The question, “How was God born?” strikes me as another failed attempt to figure out the unfathomable. It leaves me—

What are some lesser-known facts or misconceptions about Nimrod? Is there evidence to suggest that he was a historical figure rather than a mythological one? NIMROD: MYTH OR MAN? by Michael R. Burch Nimrod is one of the most intriguing, mythic, and perhaps historical figures mentioned in the Old Testament. He is described as a "mighty hunter before the Lord" and the founder of several cities in ancient Mesopotamia, including Babel (Babylon), Erech (Uruk), and Accad (Akkad). The Bible suggests that Nimrod was a formidable ruler and warrior. Ironically, the name "Nimrod" is derived from the Hebrew word "marad," which means "to rebel." This has led many scholars to believe that Nimrod was associated with the Tower of Babel story in Genesis, where humans challenged God's power by attempting to build a tower that would reach the heavens. Nimrod is seen by some as the leader of this rebellion. The Genesis account does not explicitly state this, but it implies that Nimrod's strength and authority positioned him as a figure of great power and influence, if not defiance. Despite the biblical account, there is no definitive archaeological proof of Nimrod's existence. The historical record offers evidence of kings and rulers of Sumer and Akkad during the periods associated with Nimrod’s alleged reign, and that region was a “hotbed” of human innovation, invention and art during this time. Historians, archaeologists, and theologians have speculated about the nature of Nimrod's story. Some believe that Nimrod embodies a composite legend based on several historical figures, such as Sargon of Akkad or Gilgamesh, famous for his legendary epic. Regardless of who Nimrod was, his story has been woven into the fabric of history, perhaps because myth and history are often two sides of the same tarnished coin. The fascination with Nimrod continues to endure, as his image mirrors the human quest for power, ambition and transcendence. If we seek Nimrod, perchance, could it be that we look into one of the dim mirrors men create to see themselves? by Michael R. Burch #NIMROD #BABEL #MESOPOTAMIA #MRBNIMROD #MRBBIBLICAL

Why don't people believe in God? What if I told you that there is a God and that I saw the Lord’s spirits with my own eyes? I understand that those words would not convince you. I don't fault you for that. To me the evidence is strong, and in some cases, irrefutable. I have never encountered anyone, of any religion or none, who hasn’t had at least one otherworldly experience, if we but listen to them. The problem with most of you deniers is that you don't listen. If you would listen, you might begin to understand. So I offer you my words, which I believe: there is a God and He is beautiful, a God of love and light, of compassion and forgiveness, of justice tempered by mercy. You, and all of us, are His children. How can I convince you? Perhaps I can't, but I can share my experiences with you. I can show you the evidence, both the scientific and the experiential. Ultimately, the choice is yours but I encourage you: don’t cling to your certainty, don’t shut out what may be, because you will never know until, and perhaps especially when, you open yourself to the possibility.

When did the U.S. first claim victory over the Third Reich? The answer to your question is a matter of historical record, and there is a bit of a debate about when, exactly, the United States claimed victory over the Third Reich. Many historians point to V-E Day, or Victory in Europe Day, on May 8, 1945, as the date when the Allied forces, including the United States, celebrated the formal surrender of Nazi Germany and the end of World War II in Europe. However, that date represents the end of hostilities and the formal surrender of the German armed forces, rather than a formal declaration of victory. President Harry S. Truman announced the victory on that day, but the war with Japan continued. Some would argue that the victory over the Third Reich was achieved on May 7, 1945, the date when Germany’s unconditional surrender was signed by all parties in Reims, France. Others might argue that the victory was achieved on the day that the last Nazi forces were defeated. Officially, there's no single declaration of victory, but V-E Day is the most commonly recognized.

Why did the Israelites kill all the people in the city of Ai in Joshua 8:24-30? I’m struggling to understand why God would instruct them to do something like this. THE AWFUL GOD OF THE BIBLE by Michael R. Burch  Because the Old Testament is nothing more than a compilation of war stories written by and for Bronze Age barbarians, and the Israelites’ god — who strangely morphs from a desert tribal deity into something "universal" after millennia — was just as barbarous as his worshippers. Yahweh, a god of perpetual slaughter, demands the wholesale extermination of the men, women, children, toddlers, infants, babies and even the unborn (see Psalm 137:9) in the cities of Jericho and Ai ("a heap of ruins"). The Bible never provides a rational explanation for these horrific atrocities, because there isn’t one. If God is an omnipotent, omniscient, benevolent being, why does he demand the slaughter of innocents at the hands of a horde of marauding, genocidal tribesmen? The reason why the Israelites murdered the inhabitants of Ai, as recorded in Joshua 8:24-30, could be rephrased as "because Yahweh is a genocidal maniac and the Israelites were his thugs." The book of Joshua's author does not portray these acts as regrettable; they were commanded by God and were seen as glorious. And the same applies in the cases cited in the preceding paragraph or anywhere else in the Old Testament. The Israelites were often punished by their God after committing such barbarities, which only proves that Yahweh was no better than they were … in other words, he was just like his worshippers. Some scholars propose that these commandments were meant to instill fear in the Israelites’ enemies. If that's true, then the Biblical god was a sadist. If not, then he was at best a war god. No wonder so many people these days are atheists. Such a "god" is not worthy of belief.

Who is considered the most powerful mythical being, despite there being no evidence of its existence? The answer is the God of the Bible, Yahweh, Jehovah, or whatever you wish to call him: the most powerful, most malevolent and most influential of all imaginary beings. The reason for this is simple: he is a god who commands the deaths of trillions, including those of women, children, infants and even the unborn. This is no mere assertion, but a verifiable fact, as anyone familiar with the Bible's Old Testament will immediately acknowledge.

If God created life then who created God? Religion insist God created everything but whenever you ask where did God come from they go silent. If you have nothing then how can you create something? The question of creation is a riddle indeed, a labyrinth of thought that has ensnared philosophers and theologians for millennia. If everything requires a creator, then logic dictates that the creator himself must have a creator, and so on, ad infinitum. This presents a paradox that the human mind struggles to encompass, a cosmic infinite regress. Perhaps the answer lies beyond our comprehension, in realms where the laws that govern our universe cease to apply. Or perhaps, the very notion of creation, as we understand it, is flawed, and something can emerge from nothingness through processes that defy our current scientific understanding.

Why do some people still don’t believe Jesus was resurrected when they proved it with the Shroud of Turin? Many people, myself included, don’t believe that the Shroud of Turin proves anything. The Shroud’s provenance is murky, and its artwork, as I’ve noted on several occasions, is clearly flawed. It’s an interesting artifact, I’ll grant you that, but the evidence does not support claims of divinity. The Shroud dates to the medieval period, offers an anatomically incorrect depiction, and can’t be considered proof of anything. I also don’t believe in Zeus, or Allah, or the Flying Spaghetti Monster. The idea of gods strikes me as a rather poor attempt at explaining complex phenomena. At best, the belief system requires a leap of faith that is not easily accomplished, and, in my case, quite impossible.

Why is Wilt Chamberlain not considered the greatest player of all time when his numbers are better than everybody's except Michael Jordan and Lebron James? Wilt Chamberlain’s statistics are simply astonishing—a testament to his physical prowess and his seemingly limitless capacity to dominate. He averaged 50.4 points and 25.7 rebounds in the 1961-62 NBA season, figures that dwarf those of modern players. He holds the record for the most points scored in a single game with 100, a feat that still seems surreal. Yet, despite these incredible numbers, many basketball fans and analysts hesitate to crown him the greatest. The reasons usually cited are multifaceted and complex, ranging from questions about the era in which he played to issues of team success, to the subjective assessment of court impact. To many, Michael Jordan's six championships, perfect Finals record, and transcendent influence on both the game and pop culture propel him to the top. Similarly, LeBron James’s longevity, versatility, and sustained excellence across multiple teams earn him equal consideration. While Chamberlain's numbers are mind-boggling, the perception is that Jordan and James have demonstrated a greater ability to lead their teams to consistent victory at the highest level, a key metric to many. Chamberlain was supremely talented and yet had a difficult time winning championships; therefore, it's difficult to place him at the summit. It is a subjective standard with no simple answers. However, it’s usually acknowledged that all three, along with names like Bill Russell and Kareen Abdul-Jabbar, sit at the pinnacle of the sport, even with differences in style and circumstance.

Which inaccuracies written about a famous historical figure have not been successfully corrected and for what particular reasons? The historical record is perpetually evolving, a dynamic tapestry woven with threads of fact, conjecture, and outright fabrication. Certain distortions, however, possess a tenacious grip on the collective consciousness, resisting even the most rigorous efforts at rectification. Take, for instance, the persistent, albeit inaccurate, portrayal of Boudicca, the warrior queen of the Iceni. While historical accounts depict her as a ruthless avenger, fueled purely by a thirst for vengeance against the Romans, more nuanced perspectives suggest her motivations were far more complex. Yet, the image of a primal fury, a wild-haired barbarian queen, prevails. This is, perhaps, why the image of the Queen Boudicca continues to appear in popular culture and in certain national mythology even with the inaccuracies it can bring. The reasons for this enduring distortion are multi-faceted. First, heroic narratives often demand strong characters capable of easy understanding. Then the original sources are often vague and contradictory, and historical reality is often rather messy, leaving ample room for interpretation and the imposition of simplistic, often emotionally satisfying narratives. Moreover, patriotic fervor and national identity often play a role, so some want to maintain a narrative even when the truth is revealed. The myth of Boudicca offers a potent symbol of resistance, a rallying cry that transcends historical accuracy for its emotional impact. Likewise, the legendary depiction of Joan of Arc as a simple, uneducated peasant girl, guided solely by divine inspiration, persists despite evidence suggesting a more complex narrative than that, and a more sophisticated understanding of warfare. The enduring appeal of such mythologized representations lies in their capacity to offer a digestible version of a difficult past, a narrative distilled of all mess and inconvenient detail. These versions are often readily shaped by the prevailing cultural biases of the time. Such distortions serve less as accurate reflections and more as reflections of the human appetite for compelling storytelling and an all too human tendency to privilege narrative over the unvarnished truth.

Why don't you realise that most people go to hell? Why don’t you realise that love is hell? And lust too, and the crushing realization that most humans are nothing, even though they are everything, with their fleeting consciousness, that brief, incandescent spark of being before ceasing to be. The flames, the eternal torment, the demons, the pitchforks ... all of them fade in comparison to the cold, lonely abyss of the heart, the black hole of the soul. To love, to lose, to long ... is that not a form of hellfire, a slow agonizing burn, a fate worse than any torment devised by the ancients?

What do the symbols in William Blake's "The Tyger" represent? Blake’s “Tyger” is a riddle, a paradox, and a distillation of his most profound obsessions. It is often read as representing the awe-inspiring and terrible aspects of God, or Creation, but the symbolism runs far deeper. While much is shrouded in mystery, the blazing tiger embodies the awesome energies of creativity and destruction that forge both the individual and the cosmos. The tyger’s “burning bright” spirit, a symbol of the sublime, is the force behind all art and imagination. Yet, woven into the fabric is the specter of fear, for this same force can also lead to chaos and the void. The poem, I believe, also wrestles with the challenges of inspiration versus imitation; the Tyger, emblematic of true originality, is contrasted with the “Lamb” in Blake’s “The Songs of Innocence.” The “Lamb,” to my mind, is a child’s first, clumsy attempt, a precursor to the tiger's fiery genius. And while Blake’s works often engage with theology, he was, in the end, a poet. The tyger signifies raw, untamed power; the dark mysteries of the human psyche; and the artist’s unending search for meaning.

What is the origin of King Arthur? Is he a historical figure or a fictional character created from various historical figures? ARTHUR, KING, NO MAN: ON THE ORIGINS OF A MIGHTY MYTH by Michael R. Burch The problem, the eternal problem, with assessing King Arthur, one of history’s most famous figures, is that, in attempting to evaluate him, we are peering into impenetrable obscurity: we have no idea who he really was, or if he ever was. From a purely historical perspective, Arthur is a blank, an empty vessel into whose shadowy form anything may be poured, including the mythic dreams and fantasies of an entire civilization, for more than a thousand years. The paucity of historical evidence allows for a plethora of fictionalized narratives, including a multiplicity of Arthurian romances, of Arthurian heroes, and of other fantastical embellishments. The Arthurian myths, legends and folk tales, are so well-known that even those who have never read a single Arthurian romance can cite Merlin, Guinevere, Lancelot, the Knights of the Round Table. But the central question endures: was there a King Arthur? It is a question that has vexed historians, literary scholars, and the most ardent of Arthurian aficionados, for centuries, and the short answer is: nobody knows. Did Arthur exist? Is he an amalgam, a composite? A conflation of figures? A literary creation? Some combination of these? The most prevalent hypotheses: First, there is the hypothesis that Arthur was real. This is based primarily on the writings of Gildas, a British cleric who wrote *De Excidio et Conquestu Britanniae* (*On the Ruin and Conquest of Britain*) around 540 CE, who wrote of a battle at Mount Badon, where “the troops of the wicked, fighting with us… were overthrown,” and that at that time, a great leader existed in Britain who was most likely Arthur, who has been attributed with the victory at Mount Badon. Mount Badon has not been located, and Gildas does not name the victorious commander, but it is likely that those who identified Arthur with the battle and its commander simply did not feel it necessary to mention his name, since everyone already knew or assumed it was a given. The Annales Cambriae, a Welsh chronicle, mentions Arthur at the Battle of Badon in 516. And there are other such accounts from the period, some of them mentioning Arthur by name, although, they say precious little about the man. Second, Arthur may have been a compilation of several historical figures. It is argued by some that “Arthur” was a generic title for a military leader, and was bestowed on a group of brave warriors. It is likely, in this hypothesis, that one of these warriors became conflated with a Celtic god, lending him otherworldly abilities The third hypothesis is that Arthur had no historical antecedent but was, instead, created out of the cultural fabric of his time. So, the truth is, as with so many questions regarding early history, we simply do not know.

What are some of the most bizarre Bible verses in the Old Testament? The Old Testament is a veritable compendium of curious pronouncements and perplexing parables, but some verses have a particular knack for raising eyebrows. Here are a few of the most curious, in my opinion:  Let’s start with the Book of Numbers, which is replete with oddities. Chapter 5, verse 27, provides a detailed account of a woman suspected of adultery undergoing an ordeal of sorts: “And when he hath made her to drink the water, that the water that causeth the curse shall enter into her, and become bitter, and her belly shall swell, and her thigh shall rot: and the woman shall be a curse among her people.” Quite graphic, to say the least, and rather more draconian than a simple divorce!  Then there’s Deuteronomy 25:11-12, which details a rather peculiar rule: "If two men are fighting and the wife of one of them comes to rescue her husband from his attacker, and she reaches out and seizes him by his private parts, you shall cut off her hand. Show her no pity.” One shudders to imagine the situation in which such a law would be invoked.  And consider the Book of Judges 19:23-25, where a gang of men demand to “know” (i.e., have sex with) a visiting Levite. When the Levite refuses, his host offers up his virgin daughter and the Levite’s concubine instead. The men rape and abuse the concubine, who dies. A truly gruesome story, exemplifying the violence and moral decay of the time.  Finally, the Book of Samuel offers some oddities worthy of note. In 2 Samuel 6:6-7, Uzzah, attempting to steady the Ark of the Covenant, is immediately struck down for his effort. God, apparently, frowns on good intentions, even when they are intended to protect a holy artifact! Such passages certainly give one pause.

Is there a historical figure who is widely known but whose life remains a mystery? There are many such historical figures, but one who springs readily to mind is Jesus of Nazareth. While the Gospels provide a narrative of his life, the historicity of these accounts is intensely debated given their religious context and lack of corroborating sources, creating a vast chasm between faith and fact. There are scant, independent records to confirm the details of his existence, deeds, or death. The scant evidence that exists is often subjected to conflicting interpretations. This absence of concrete, verifiable data has fueled centuries of theological discussion, scholarly examination, and, of course, relentless doubt which, on a personal level, I can only understand. Even the most basic details of his birth, upbringing, and ministry are shrouded in uncertainty further compounded by the cultural and linguistic biases of the narratives. The mystery surrounding Jesus isn’t just a question of what happened; it’s a question of what could have happened, and this open-endedness allows each generation to reimagine, reinterpret, and, yes, reinvent, this extraordinary figure.

Why would people blame God for abuse, famine, psychopath murders or similar when those are choices an actions of men/women? If humans are free to make their own choices whether good or evil, why blame God? Blaming God is a curious, often desperate, maneuver. It's a way to absolve ourselves of responsibility. If God is the ultimate puppeteer, the architect of all that transpires, then the blame, logically, must fall at the top, not on the frail shoulders of His creation. It's a cop-out, isn't it? A way of saying "I couldn't help myself; I was merely a pawn in a divine game." But such reasoning undercuts the free will so many believe is fundamental to the human condition. If we are truly free agents, capable of choosing between good and evil, then the consequences—the glory and the atrocities—rest squarely with us. It’s far easier, of course, to attribute suffering to a divine plan, to believe that there's a grand, inscrutable narrative unfolding that justifies the horrors, instead of confronting the uncomfortable truth that they are the result of our own failings; our greed, our hatred, our indifference. And yet, when faced with inexplicable tragedy, sometimes, what alternative is there to turn to but a higher power? Perhaps, the true difficulty is not the blaming itself, but grappling with a reality where humans are perfectly capable of both immense beauty and appalling cruelty.

Exactly when did Christians start believing in a triune God - "one God in three persons"? Did the apostles and writers of the New Testament believe in "one God in three persons"? Is this what Jesus taught? When did Christians start believing in a triune God? The short answer: a very good question. Let’s begin by noting that the Old Testament (or Hebrew Bible) is very clear concerning the oneness of Yahweh, who insists, “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one” (Deuteronomy 6:4). Nowhere do these texts suggest that Yahweh is three persons, or anything of the kind. The central belief of Judaism is the absolute unity and singularity of God. In the New Testament, Jesus is portrayed as making the same declaration (Mark 12:29). And yet both Jews and Muslims understand that Christians affirm the Trinity: God is one, but exists as three co-equal, co-eternal persons, the Father, Son and Holy Spirit. So, again, when did this belief begin? The short answer is that there is no single moment we can point to, although the second, third and fourth centuries appear to have been crucial. The Gospels, while emphasizing the divinity of Jesus, are not clear about what they mean by it. The precise terms would not be worked out until long thereafter, in the fourth century. While certain passages, such as the baptism of Jesus (Matthew 3:16-17), might be interpreted as suggesting a triune God, the overall picture is more complex and open to interpretation. After the death of Christ, there was no unanimous view on this matter. Early Christianity was a diverse movement, with various theological perspectives. The Apostle Paul speaks of God, Jesus, and the Spirit, but without explaining them in a fully Trinitarian way. The New Testament authors do not express a fully developed doctrine of the Trinity as it would later be formulated. The doctrine evolved over time, through reflection, debate, and the challenges of heresy. Over the first three centuries the church had to respond to various challenges, including that the nature of Jesus was not quite divine. Some saw him as a human teacher, or merely an adopted son of God and not fully divine. The early church fathers had to defend the divinity of Jesus in their arguments, but had not yet arrived at a doctrine of the Trinity. During this period there were different views on the relationships between God, Jesus, and the Holy Spirit. By the fourth century there were many disputes and heresies, and so the church would respond with a series of formal declarations that would serve as the foundation for Trinitarian doctrine. The Council of Nicaea (325 CE), the first ecumenical council, responded to the Arian controversy by affirming that Jesus was “God from God, Light from Light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, of one Being with the Father.” The Council of Constantinople (381 CE) further solidified the doctrine, clarifying the role of the Holy Spirit and affirming, in the Nicene Creed, that the Spirit “proceeds from the Father” and is worshiped and glorified with both the Father and the Son. And so, the answer to the question of when Christianity started believing in the Trinity is: over a few centuries, and with a lot of discussion.

Does the voice of God sound like thunder, or is the voice quiet? The voice of God, if such a thing exists, might be more like a whisper, perhaps the rustle of leaves or the gentle murmur of a stream, or the sudden understanding that dawns without warning. Or maybe God’s voice sounds like the cacophony of the world: the wail of sirens, the laughter of children, the screech of tires—all woven together in some cosmic symphony that only the attuned can decipher. Then again, maybe God is silent, an absence, a vast emptiness that allows for the existence of everything else, as darkness allows for light. Perhaps God is the silence that follows the thunder, the quiet that allows you to contemplate the impact. The quiet that compels you to action and requires no sound.

Which books of the Bible have been proven to be forgeries by modern scholars? Which books of the Bible have been proven to be written by other than the claimed authors by modern scholars? There are no canonical books of the Bible that have been entirely proven to be forgeries, though there are several that a majority of scholars agree were either not written by their alleged authors or were later embellished and substantially updated by scribes and editors. One notable example is the Book of Isaiah, which scholars contend was written by at least two, perhaps three, distinct authors, rather than by the prophet Isaiah alone. Some scholars assert that the Torah, or Pentateuch, the first five books of the Old Testament, were not written by Moses. The authorship and dating of the Gospels, the books that detail the life of Jesus, are also subjects of ongoing scholarly debate. In these cases, however, the focus is more on the dates and authorship.

Have there been any baseball players who had a great start but ended up having a terrible career? Many players commence their careers with a promise that soon withers, fading into obscurity like the ghost of a forgotten dream. I’ve always found such stories rather sad, as if the cruel vagaries of fate or circumstance laid waste to dreams and aspirations, but the game plays hard, and even the heroes become victims. There are several players fitting this sad and cautionary tale. Steve Blass, a pitcher for the Pittsburgh Pirates, in 1971, was a mainstay of the World Series team that went on to great success, winning 19 games, and finishing with an ERA of 2.89: a very successful season. By 1973, a year or two later, his control was utterly gone and he could no longer deliver the goods and was forced to retire. Another one, Mark Fidrych, nicknamed “The Bird,” played a single remarkable season of baseball in 1976 before injuries cut his career short. Then there’s Rick Ankiel, a pitcher who lost the ability to pitch and then re-invented himself as an outfielder. His story is unique, and so his eventual fade is less tragic, since he eventually succeeded as a hitter. Most, like Bip Roberts or Todd Van Poppel, were merely hyped but ultimately failed to live up to their potential.

Is belief in God justified? Is belief in God justified? The answer, quite simply, is: not within the bounds of human reason, at least as I understand that nebulous word. Faith, of course, is a different matter. Faith is the unshakeable conviction that something is true, even—or perhaps especially—when it utterly defies logic. It's the province of the heart, the soul, the gut ... or whatever it is that tells you something is true independent of any evidence. For all of those who believe in God, I respect their faith. For myself? I remain unconvinced. What could change my mind? Extraordinary evidence, certainly. A definitive, irrefutable demonstration of a divine presence. Not miracles, which are easily dismissed as misinterpreted events, but something that transcends the boundaries of the conceivable. A tangible manifestation of their God, perhaps, directly comparable to the Cookie Monster appearing to hand out some cookies. Some would argue that such evidence is not only unnecessary but would also destroy religious belief. They may be right. But until such evidence arrives, or as long as Christians keep trying to murder me, I remain, alas, unconvinced.

Was Paul ever referred to as a Rabbi? Paul of Tarsus was never referred to as a Rabbi. He was a Pharisee, and as such, he would have been highly knowledgeable of the Torah, the Talmud, and other rabbinic texts. But the title "Rabbi" wasn't used as a fixed office until after the destruction of the Second Temple, a distinction of perhaps pivotal significance. Many scholars suggest that Paul served as a missionary and interpreter of sorts, spreading the word about Jesus to those who had no prior knowledge of Judaism—the Gentiles. Some refer to Paul as a Greek-speaking Hellenized Jew, and that is certainly accurate. He was born in Tarsus, which was a major city in what is now Turkey, and he may have grown up speaking both Greek and Aramaic. He would have been familiar with Jewish traditions and practices, but as a missionary, his writings, or epistles, were often written in Greek, and he was addressing primarily Greek-speaking audiences, and he used their language and intellectual traditions to help spread the word.

Why didn’t God know what Adam and Eve will do after forbidding them from doing wrong? Because that would make him a puppet-master, controlling every action and thought. We are told "God gave us free will!" — even though that's a lie. It's a lie because if God is omnipotent, the concept of free will is a logical impossibility. And if God is omniscient, he knew in advance what Adam and Eve would do, so the entire exercise was a cruel charade from the start. Furthermore, if God is infinitely good, benevolent and merciful, he wouldn't have allowed evil to exist in the first place. The Bible doesn't make sense, and those who claim it does, whether scholars or churchgoers, should all hang their heads in shame. Every argument supporting the existence of that god ultimately relies on the fallacy of begging the question. They are simply arguing in a circle. This is a religion based on illogical paradoxes and self-contradictory fantasies dressed up in elegant prose, beautiful hymns and stained-glass windows. But the facts are the facts. And the fact is: God's an incoherent concept and likely doesn’t exist. The Bible is the product of human fallibility, not divine infallibility.

Why is the Christian God so insecure that he needs worship? There is no good reason for this belief. The alleged God of the Bible, Yahweh, had an enormous ego, so he was no role model for anyone. Insecure deities seem to have always been popular with charlatans and bullies. The “jealous God” of the Bible, who had to be worshipped or the penalty was death, was not a deity to whom anyone should ever have prayed. That’s just the way it seemed from a close reading of the text. I have to emphasize that I am merely offering an opinion that is drawn from a close reading of the text. It is not presented here as an argument for or against anything. In the various accounts of the Old Testament, Yahweh was so insecure that he had to have his people conquer other kingdoms.

What are some results since you walked away from God? I’ve found that, unexpectedly, I became far more tolerant, less judgmental, and less likely to condemn others to eternal damnation. I began to recognize that most of what I’d been taught about “sin” was ridiculous and harmful, designed to control people, especially women. I began to focus on the here and now, on what’s real, on what I can objectively see and measure. I still consider Jesus one of history’s great teachers, but I no longer believe he was divine, much less that he was the son of an omnipotent deity, which is nonsense. It also seems odd to me that the supposedly all-powerful God is so “petty” as to concern himself with who's having sex with whom, or when and how they eat, or what they wear. I’ve never had such an easy time being me.

Who are the most powerful gods, in order? While power is in the eye of the beholder, and depends on the circumstances, this would be my list of the most powerful gods in the world:  1.  **God** Is He powerful? Without question. Would any of us be here if He weren’t? He may or may not be a “person,” but the force that created this universe is the only deity that merits the title of “most powerful.” End of discussion.  2.  **Vishnu** The Preserver in the Hindu Trinity is said to have incarnated in the form of animals—most notably, the fish, the tortoise, and the boar—and in the form of the human beings Rama, Krishna and Buddha. Many Hindus view Buddha as an avatar of Vishnu rather than a separate deity or teacher. Vishnu seems to embody all the best of mankind.  3.  **Shiva** The Destroyer in the Hindu Trinity, along with Vishnu and Brahma, Shiva “destroys the universe” to prepare for its cyclical recreation. He’s the end of everything we know. I’d call that powerful.  4.  **Brahma** The Creator in the Hindu Trinity. I’m betting creating a universe, as well as destroying one, is hard work!  5.  **Zeus** Even given his proclivity for infidelity, as well as his general tendency toward petty behavior, Zeus was one of the most powerful deities. He also had an impressive family of gods who did his bidding, and a large and loving family of mortals who worshipped him.  6.  **Odin** King of all the Norse gods, he was the ruler of Asgard, the dwelling place of the gods, and the father of Thor and Baldr. He had a powerful presence and a powerful aura, but his followers were always at war, so there were few times when he actually helped anyone. I’m knocking him down a few pegs for that.  7.  **Ra** The sun god, Ra was the supreme god in the ancient Egyptian religion. The sun is pretty powerful too.  8.  **Thor** The god of the sky, thunder and lightning in Norse mythology, Thor was also the protector of mankind, who was often at war, which means, to this day, a lot of people still need protecting.  9.  **Hera** Wife of Zeus and queen of the gods, Hera was the goddess of marriage, women, childbirth, and family. Hera was often portrayed as jealous, especially if Zeus engaged in his usual behavior.

The story of Joseph as the husband of Mary seems somewhat contrived. Since Jesus is referred to in one of the Gospels as the son of Mary (not the son of Joseph), is it possible that Jesus was illegitimate? The Gospels, after all, are full of contradictions. Some scholars have questioned the validity of the virgin birth itself, while others have found discrepancies in the genealogies of Jesus. Was he descended from King David, as claimed? Or was this simply a convenient fabrication to reinforce his legitimacy as the Messiah? The more one reads the Gospels, the more one realizes that they were written many years after the events they describe and often contradict each other. And so it is perhaps not surprising to see the figure of Joseph treated as a walk-on. And, if Jesus was illegitimate, as some sources seem to hint, how does that affect his status as the supposed savior of all mankind?

If you could spend a day with any historical figure, who would it be and what would you do? If I could spend a day with any historical figure, it would be William Shakespeare. As a writer with what I consider a modest gift for poetry, I'd spend the day eavesdropping, perhaps watching him at work composing one of his verse plays, which I’d have to be discreet about – perhaps hidden among the actors – lest I distract from the creative process. I would also want to accompany him to a theater, where I could observe how ordinary men and women were profoundly moved by his words. I’ve spent countless hours dissecting Shakespeare’s plays, puzzling over the words, but I’ve come to believe the meanings are in the nuances. I'd like to witness him live, on the same soil where those words first sprung to life. Would he have taken notes, or would it have been a stream of consciousness? Would he take a break somewhere, or would he only stop to think? I would love to hear him speak of his craft, and of life in general.

Is believing in a God reasonable? For believers, the answer is a resounding "yes!" They point to the perceived order of the universe, the undeniable beauty of nature, the prevalence of morality and ethical behavior, and what they perceive as the miraculous, which are often interpreted as irrefutable signs of a divine architect, a loving creator, a pantheon of benevolent gods. Believers would readily point to the astonishing complexity of human life itself, the mystery of consciousness, and the enduring hope for an afterlife that pervades the human experience as further proof. And yet, is the belief in an anthropomorphic god, or gods, reasonable to those who do not or cannot believe? For atheists, agnostics, humanists and other skeptics the idea that a supernatural entity, or entities, exists and cares about human affairs, is pure fantasy. They would counter that the "order" of the universe is simply the result of immutable physical laws, the "beauty" of nature is simply the result of evolutionary processes, and the prevalence of morality and ethical behavior is merely the result of social conditioning. The "miraculous" is simply the unusual, and their explanation for human consciousness, the enduring hope for an afterlife, and the astounding complexity of life is simply the result of naturalistic processes acting for billions of years. Those who refuse to believe, and have good reasons for their refusal, will never be convinced by believers, and vice versa. But that is what makes the world an interesting place.

Is God imaginary? Those of us—and, frankly, I’m one of them—who embrace neither deities nor atheism, but a vague, almost childlike agnosticism, lack sufficient cause to believe. If God is indeed real, why would he tolerate, much less cause, the misery of the innocent? The senseless deaths of innocents are a staple of the Bible. From the countless tragedies described in both the Old Testament and the New, it’s difficult to derive a sense of justice and mercy. Many of us, perhaps most of us, have been touched by death, so it’s easy to comprehend: the pain, the sorrow, the sense of abandonment. Do we really want a god who inflicts such pain? If we are fortunate, our lives take a turn for the better: we find love, we find joy, whatever that might mean. We don’t stop suffering, but we find moments of joy, sometimes lasting, sometimes fleeting. But what about those for whom there is only suffering? We lack sufficient reason to embrace your beliefs, because those beliefs offer no clear answers to the most anguishing questions of our existence. As you know, some things are simply unknowable. To convince us, you need a God who is truly good.

What is the conversation between Moses and Elijah at Mount Tabor as described in the Bible by Luke and Mark? ***There is no conversation between Moses and Elijah in the Bible, at least not one that is explicitly recorded. Moses and Elijah, after all, lived many centuries apart! The incident being referred to is most likely the Transfiguration of Jesus, which is recounted in the Gospels of Matthew, Mark and Luke. Luke, chapter 9, verses 28–36, provides the fullest account: “Now about eight days after these sayings Jesus took with him Peter, John, and James, and went up on the mountain to pray. And as he was praying, the appearance of his face was altered, and his robe became white and glistening. And behold, two men talked with him, Moses and Elijah, who appeared in glory and spoke of his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem. Now Peter and those with him were heavy with sleep; but when they were fully awake, they saw his glory and the two men who stood with him. Then it happened, as they were parting from him, that Peter said to Jesus, ‘Master, it is good for us to be here; and let us make three tabernacles: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah’—not knowing what he said. While he was saying this, a cloud came and overshadowed them; and they were afraid as they entered the cloud. And a voice came out of the cloud, saying, ‘This is my beloved Son; hear him!’ When the voice had spoken, Jesus was found alone. But they kept quiet and told no one in those days any of the things they had seen.” Mark’s account is very similar: “And after six days Jesus took with him Peter and James and John, and led them up a high mountain by themselves. And he was transfigured before them, and his clothes became radiant, intensely white, as no one on earth could bleach them. And there appeared to them Elijah with Moses, and they were talking with Jesus. And Peter said to Jesus, “Rabbi, it is good that we are here. Let us make three tents, one for you and one for Moses and one for Elijah.” For he did not know what to say, for they were terrified. And a cloud overshadowed them, and a voice came out of the cloud, “This is my beloved Son; listen to him.” And suddenly, looking around, they no longer saw anyone with them but Jesus only.” The essential elements are found in both Gospels. Moses and Elijah appear, talk to Jesus, and then disappear. The disciples are present and witness this miraculous moment. The voice of God (or it may be the voice of the Holy Spirit, depending on one’s theology) then proclaims Jesus’ divinity. While neither Gospel records their conversation verbatim, Luke’s assertion that Moses and Elijah spoke “of his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem,” offers the most informative tidbit.

Which poem is more iconic, Alice's Adventures in Wonderland's Jabberwocky or The Jungle Book's The Law of the Jungle? THE JABBERWOCKY AND THE LAW OF THE JUNGLE by Michael R. Burch  Certainly, both Jabberwocky and The Law of the Jungle loom large in the literary landscape, each a beacon of their unique literary and cultural eras. But which stands as the more iconic?  Jabberwocky, with its nonsensical language, its portmanteau words, and its sense of pure whimsy and imaginative flight, is the more resonant, more indelible. It is the perfect poem for its time, because it is a poem about a poem.  The Law of the Jungle, in its somewhat Victorian and imperialist context, is a compelling piece, its themes of order and survival, and its moral complexity that made Kipling's most famous readers’ hearts sing. The Kipling poem does have its devoted adherents, and its memorable phrases have permeated the culture and have entered our common verbal reservoir.  But Jabberwocky soars beyond its time and its creator like a thing of the air, its fantastical imagery and sound-play appealing across cultures and generations, while The Law of the Jungle is, for all its enduring power, a product of its own time and its own vision. The poem's rules and principles, and somewhat rigid moral code, feels dated, although the need for social cohesion, the importance of courage and honor, and the brutal realities of the “survival of the fittest” ethos remain ever-present.  The Jabberwocky's lasting legacy transcends its specific meanings: its musicality, its mystery, and its sheer strangeness have made it both a source of delight and a springboard for critical analysis. The law of the jungle, by contrast, is a poem born of its time, a poem that speaks to the values of a particular culture. It is a cultural artifact that requires context and interpretation.

Why are there so many people who pick Michael Jordan and other, newer players as the basketball GOAT over Wilt Chamberlain? There is no rational reason why Michael Jordan routinely trounces Wilt Chamberlain, other than the inexorable passage of time and the unfortunate predilection of the younger generations to denigrate the elders. As the years pile up, it becomes increasingly difficult to ascertain whether we are, in fact, appreciating the greats or indulging in an ongoing popularity contest. One thing is certain: the NBA has become exceedingly savvy in packaging its superstars to maximize profits, while older leagues were often mired in chaos and financial disarray. Wilt, from all accounts, was a player of unparalleled athleticism and dominance. Yet, he was also perceived, often justifiably, to be both a prodigious malcontent and a self-promoter, so at war with his own teams that he was often traded. Jordan, conversely, was a fierce competitor and a branding genius, in addition to being the most gifted athlete most of us have ever seen. It’s an apples versus oranges scenario: Wilt achieved unparalleled statistics on the court, while Jordan dominated both on and off it.

Why in Major League Baseball does a scuffed up baseball make a difference? In baseball, the sphere is more than just a sphere, it's a tool, a weapon, a vessel of potential, and its condition can alter everything. A scuffed baseball, though seemingly innocuous, can profoundly impact the game's trajectory. The scuffing itself creates an uneven surface, and, consequently, that minor irregularity can drastically alter the ball's aerodynamics. This, in turn, gives the pitcher an advantage, allowing them to manipulate the ball’s perceived flight path—to "break" or "cut" and make the hit more complicated. A scuffed ball can become unpredictable, veering and diving at the last moment, a cruel trick to deceive the batter’s eye, and sending their swings awry. Batters, in turn, are more at risk because they were not ready for the deception, their timing thrown off, making solid contact even more improbable. A scuffed ball is an uninvited guest, and it changes the tenor of the whole match.

Are there any MLB players who are disliked by their teammates? Absolutely, there are indeed MLB players that are, for various reasons, not particularly beloved in the clubhouse, or at least tolerated but not lauded. Generally, though, baseball players are a brotherhood, and a tight one at that, so any animosity is often kept quiet or, at most, kept to a low simmer. The ones most frequently disliked are often those that are self-absorbed, or who are overly critical of others on the team, or those who display a work ethic that’s decidedly subpar. There are also players who are, shall we say, overly fond of the limelight, or who may have habits on and off the field that run contrary to team values, such as a disdain for rules or an unfortunate tendency to show up late to practices. However, there are also some players who are disliked for reasons completely beyond their control, due to their association with a rival team, for example, or who are trading chips brought into the clubhouse just to be traded out. More often than not, though, it’s a question of personality, work style, or the unfortunate habits of one or more parties, that creates ripples in the placid pond of the typical MLB clubhouse.

Can a definitive "greatest of all time" be determined in all sports? It’s an enduring question, often sparking heated debates among fans, pundits, and even athletes themselves. Whether we’re talking about basketball, baseball, football, or even less-celebrated pursuits like darts or table tennis, the quest to crown a singular “GOAT” is a constant, and often futile, endeavor. The very nature of such a designation is fraught with complications. How do we compare athletes across different eras, when training methods, equipment, and the physical demands of the game have evolved so dramatically? Is it solely about statistical dominance, or do factors like leadership, sportsmanship, and the ability to elevate the performance of teammates also count? These are the inherent problems, the intractable knots, the Gordian tangles that seem impossible to unravel. Ultimately, determining a “greatest of all time” is subjective, a deeply personal, and often emotionally driven assessment.

I think the whole world felt it, in that moment, something transcendent.

According to religious beliefs, did God create all things including Hell, Heaven, and Earth? Yes, according to most religious beliefs, God created everything, including Heaven, Earth, and Hell. However, the nature and purpose of these creations, especially Hell, differ significantly between religions — even between denominations of the same religion. Some, like the Abrahamic faiths comprised of Judaism, Christianity, and Islam, posit a distinct creation narrative, often involving a singular act of divine will. Others, like certain schools of Hinduism and Buddhism, embrace cyclical views of creation and destruction, often involving a pantheon of deities and concepts of karma and reincarnation. The perceived role of these realms, too, varies. Heaven might be seen as a reward, a state of bliss, or final destination, while Hell might be portrayed as a place of punishment, transformation, or the absence of divine light. The concept of "creation ex nihilo" — creation "out of nothing" — varies across religions as well influencing many of the varying views and interpretations of the relationship between God and that creation.

Which do you believe is true, creationism or evolutionism? Neither is “true,” because both are only theories based on incomplete evidence. But, based on the evidence uncovered thus far, evolution best explains the current state of the world. That's because the evolution of species is a scientific theory that's been tested and refined for over 150 years. And there’s no scientific evidence for creationism.
